utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber -- [French on English channel] -- be doing that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's actually a mix-up. We can't hear you. There's a mix-up, a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not hearing me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're getting French on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Maybe that's telling you something, Mr. Groome. Okay. I'll repeat it. I was saying the Chamber issued an order today, and I believe you'll all have received it. Tomorrow we will have a discussion on it. I don't want any discussion on it at this time. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave I would like to raise some different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Absolutely different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I am to say that in the absence of Judge Van Den Wyngaert, Judge David and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. During the cross-examination of some of OTP witnesses, both parties use OTP 65 ter Exhibit Number 177.12, which is the map of Visegrad area. So I kindly ask admission of that -- of that exhibit entire -- as entire map. And I spoke to Mr. Groome and to Mr. Alarid, there is no objection in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 2D59, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, today we bring the witness we have available today is Stephen Patrick O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How are you doing this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please state your -- excuse me. Could you please state your full name for the record, please, spelling it as well.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Stephen Patrick O'Donnell, S-t-e-p-h-e-n P-a-t-r-i-c-k O'D-o-n-n-e-l-l.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please tell the Court where and when were you born.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Chicago Illinois, 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where do you now reside?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Albuquerque, New Mexico.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, three. Two girls and a boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are their ages?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: 13, 7, and we have a brand new baby boy of 2 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please tell us about your education starting with high school.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I graduated from Grayslake High School in a northern suburb of Chicago, and went away to the Marine Corps for -- on active duty for four years. And when I got done with the Marine Corps, I went back to Chicago. I went to college for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So in post-secondary school where did you go to college?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Western Illinois University. It's in Macomb, Illinois, which is near the Mississippi river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And any other post-secondary or speciality education?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Other than the military schools that I've gone through, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through that in a second. Let's first talk about your service. Tell us about when you served for the United States Marine Corps.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I served from September of 1991 to September of 1995 on active duty, and from 1995 to 1996 in a reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: For the Marine Corps I went through boot camp in MCRD in San Diego and then was stationed just outside Memphis, Tennessee for NA school, which was my primary job in the Marine Corps, which was on the aviation side of the house, cryogenics, ground support equipment in cryogenics. And then from there I was stationed at Cherry Point, North Carolina for an advanced school, and then, finally, in Hawaii, and later at Camp Pendleton in California.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That was what advanced school?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It was the systematic breakdown of the -- basically the LOX vans that we used which produced liquid nitrogen and liquid oxygen for the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And any other specialised training that you received during the Marine Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: My last two years on active duty I was a primary marksmanship instructor for the marine Corps. I basically taught other marines how to shoot the pistol and the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was a rank or position did you achieve in the Marine Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I was a corporal which is Enlisted 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what clearance level, if any, did you hold as a marine?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As a marine I held a secret security clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why did -- does every marine hold a secret security clearance?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not every member of the US military forces hold a clearance; it depends on what occupational speciality you're in and depending on the classification that dictates to which level of clearance you hold.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you ever see combat or hostile fire during your tenure in the Marine Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about the reserve marines. I believe it was 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, during that time-frame. That was a reserve unit which was located in a suburb of northern Chicago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And any -- what were your duties during that time period?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I was basically a -- my MOS was not held at that unit so I was being kind of cross-trained, not going basically to the school, military school for a specific job. I was not required to do that time. It was inactive service time, but I chose to do it. After a year because of civilian occupation I chose to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you get any additional training?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: At the reserve centre, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Any change in rank or position?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how and why did you leave the US Marine Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I performed my contract which was four years active duty, four years inactive duty time. I was up for re-enlistment. The fields, the field that I belonged to, the job that I belonged to, there was basically the -- the promotions had been frozen due to what we classify as retreads from other MOSs coming into our job field after --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is an MOS? You said that twice.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's a military occupational specialty, is what MOS stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just for those of us that aren't used to the acronyms, would you please tell us at least once what they mean.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you receive an honourable or dishonourable discharge?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I an honourable discharge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is an honourable discharge?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: An honourable discharge is you've provided -- or gone through your time and provided good conduct for the -- for the time that you're in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you receive a positive or negative appraisal of your service?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Positive appraisal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Again it was -- times were different. The hierarchy of the Presidency, you know, who was in office. We were under a democratic ruling which is not favourable to people in the military, so I chose to leave at that time and try new avenues back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when did you -- in between returning to the military, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Worked several jobs. I was a head hunter for a company that provides positions with corporations for prior service individuals, and I worked construction my last year. Between the break in service of the three year time-frame, I went to college.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about your return to the military.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: After two semesters at Western Illinois University, I struck out and sought the advice and the help of a recruiter and decided to enlist in the United States Arm specifically for the EOD programme which is explosive ordnance disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this time I would like the Court's assistance with 1D22-0611.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what I'm just bringing up here on the screen here, Mr. O'Donnell, is a copy of your latest resume. I believe we tendered with our notice your next to most recent, and we can have it on the screen to follow or refer to as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We still have a technical difficulty, but we'll keep moving here. What I would like to do is possibly with the Court's assistance briefly as we talk about the military, can we have the court usher put something on the ELMO for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't seen these before. Is there a copy we can have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's going to be just for demonstrative purposes only. It's only meant to make a point. It will take two to three questions. We can e-mail them to you, though, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we -- we kind of looked at this a little bit earlier during our preparations, but just generally speaking, what are the things on the screen here as you know them from your military experience?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They are representation of military unit or specifically several Marine Corps unit patches, insignia patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you have opportunity during your time in the military to see these particular patches?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I've seen them. The two in the centre with VF-84 and the VF-103, I've actually seen those on the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the 4th Reconnaissance Battalion?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They're currently a reserve component of -- the 4th Reconnaissance Battalion is currently residing in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And specifically speaking, is it uncommon for the skull and crossbones or the Jolly Roger to be used in military insignias around the world?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you recognise on here patches from military outside the United States?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the bottom -- well, the bottom left Queen's Royal Lancers is a representation of, I believe, a British unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We have no further use of that one. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about EOD and your time in the army. Let's take it from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, unless there's an objection from the Prosecution because we just were tinkering with that last night, Your Honour, could we tender the sheet into evidence as representative of patches?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, anything on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, despite never having seen them before just a few seconds ago, I will not object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Take us back to 1999 and tell us what -- what you were doing and why.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I just recently left college after being in the military, and I guess you could say being in the outside world working for the government, Department Of Defence. At the age of 26 I got kind of put off from people sitting behind a desk that hadn't really been out in the world in 20 years trying to tell me how it was like in the studies and course of studies I was going through. So I left to go back in the military and enlisted in the army and left on August 17th, 1999, for Fort Jackson, South Carolina. Basically spent ten days processing paperwork and receiving uniforms. Because I was a marine from a prior service and went through the Marine Corps boot camp, I did not have to go through army boot camp. After that I was basically sent down to Eglin Air Force Base where Nav school EOD, which is the navy school of explosive ordnance disposal is run on Eglin Air Force Base, and that's in Florida.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, just before we get there, why not go back into the marines? Why choose the army?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Specifically it had everything to do with rank structure. I left the Marine Corps under good standing and held the rank of corporal, but I would have lost rank going back in and then been put at the bottom of the list for promotion, because it's unfair for me to come in after not working for three years and put me at the top of the list where all the guys have been working that are on that promotion list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so with regards to going into the army, how did you get focussed on EOD?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'd actually run into an engineer, a former guy -- a guy basically from the military who was in the civilian sector like myself, and he mentioned the EOD military speciality, the job. And when I sought the advice of the recruiter, I went forth and retested for -- to provide higher scores for jobs and was offered the EOD MOS and took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe 1D22-0611 has been released. And so tell us about going into EOD, what training you received, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's roughly a nine -- a nine-month course. But due to academics, medical, it can take longer. I arrived in September of 1999. I didn't graduate until February of 2001. I spent six months upon arrival at the school waiting for the army and the Marine Corps to decide what security clearance they were going give me because I still held a secret from the Marine Corps, but the army had started the -- basically the paperwork to grant me another clearance. So while that paperwork was trying to get ciphered through, I sat at the school basically just twiddling thumbs for six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, did he say what EOD meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But please repeat to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The acronym EOD stands for -- the acronym EOD stands for explosive ordnance disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the explosive ordnance disposal specialist course from February 2001. What specifically is the subject matter of the course?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The subject matter of the course is the understanding and the learning of the rendering safe of conventional military munitions which are your regular basically explosive devices, chemical munitions, nuclear munitions, and also improvised explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, where -- and again, where was this course held?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's at the Nav school EOD, which is the -- that acronym stands for navy school explosive ordnance disposal, which resides at Eglin Air Force Base in Fort Walton Beach, Florida. It's in the panhandle of the State.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of -- what kind of instructors were there for you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The instructors were -- they're military EOD technicians that held the rank of master badges. Basically that means that they'd been in the service working the job for over eight years. Senior NCOs, officers, basically the individuals had performed their duties for that job and had gone back to the schoolhouse to train the next generation coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And specifically -- specifically, but briefly, take us through the training you received.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It was broken down. The school itself, the curriculum was broken down into several different phases. Ordnance recognition by colour codes, bar codes, understanding the different types of ordnance that exist in the world. Your projected ordnance, your placed ordnance which would be your land-mines, being able to positively identify a grenade from an artillery piece. From there we went into the actual breakdown of different types of ordnance from -- there was a ground phase which dealt with everything that was -- you deal in type of a land war, land-mines, projectiles, rockets, grenades. We moved to air and there was two phases of that, which basically anything that's delivered by an aircraft or shot from some type of a vehicle or emplacement which would be your guided missiles, you know, large-base ordnance items. We dealt with surface-to-surface, air-to-air type of pieces of ordnance. We moved into another phase which had dealt nothing but chemical warfare, learning the -- learning what happens to individuals that are exposed to certain chemicals, how they affect you, proper procedures in approaching a piece of ordnance that is a suspected chemical, you know, how to dress up properly, decon, all that stuff. We moved into improvised explosive devices, and then the last phase was nuclear devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what specifically did you learn about post-blast exploitation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: At the schoolhouse, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. But what is post-blast exploitation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Post-blast exploitation is arriving on site after a detonation has occurred, some type of an explosive ambush has occurred; being able to cipher through all the material that's there and through fragmentation; being able to, you know, see the emplacement, how they went about initiating the device, impacts, damage done to whatever the target was. You can move forward and systematically make an assumption, technical assumption as far as what type of a device was use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And could the -- did you receive a certificate or degree, and did you complete the course?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I graduated on February 6 of 2001 and received the basic EOD badge which is a -- it's a badge that we wear on active duty on our uniforms, combat uniforms, and also our dress uniforms, and was awarded a certificate of completion of that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And specifically with the Court's assistance could we call up 1D22-0598.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And can you identify this document, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is my graduation certificate from Nav school EOD awarding me the -- the EOD badge, basic badge, and basically allowing me to provide services as an EOD technician for the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this certificate into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we bring back the resume for reference 1D22-0611.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'm just looking at your resume, and we can follow along. I note -- I note that you had other training courses in the army, notably a platoon leadership development course.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As you can -- I don't know if you noticed, but on the certificate it said SPC Stephen Patrick O'Donnell. The SPC stands for specialist, that's an E4, which is the equivalent of a corporal in the United States Marine Corp. To become a sergeant on the army side of the house as a soldier has nothing to do with the EOD side of the house. But at that level you have to go through a platoon leadership development course PLDC, which they train you basically to -- in the responsibilities of becoming the next highest rank which would be an E5 or what they consider a buck sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about the air assault course.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The air assault course is the army's course on how to basically repel out of helicopters in tactical situations, and it was necessary for me to go through that course while between deployments from Iraq and Afghanistan because we were moving to Afghanistan for a tour, and in Afghanistan due to the -- the actual geographics of the country, driving by vehicle is not always the easiest way. What normally could take five to ten minutes by aircraft could take 12 to 15 hours by vehicle due to the terrain. So we needed to basically be able to work so that we could fly or move our team and equipment in helicopters from point A to point B and be able to do it in a tactical aspect. That school provided us with the certificate and the training that allowed us to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I apologise with regards to the platoon leadership development course, did you complete that course?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That was it the Fort Benning, Georgia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you receive a certificate or something --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the air assault course?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was a 12-day course. I completed it through physical tests and received a certificate from that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I note -- for reference to the court assistance page, 3 of the resume is covering this, I note from the screen. And what about the basic NCO course?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The basic NCO course or what we call BNOC. It's again -- it's an army school that provides you the responsible -- the training and responsibilities moving from the E5 rank or sergeant to the E6 rank and staff sergeant. It is a prerequisite because at the E6 level or staff sergeant level for EOD you become the team leader of the team. So to complete that course is a prerequisite to actually being able to become a team leader for -- basically for the EOD team. That one was completed in Huntsville, Alabama, and there's numerous weeks of actual, you know, army specific NCO training and then numerous weeks of basically about half. It's split up over ten weeks, half of that is running, training scenarios as a team leader, practising your techniques and what not as far as what relates to the EOD side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And taking us back to 2001, you had said something about a difference in security clearance between the Marine Corps and the army, and there was a waiting period. Tell the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Prior to graduating from the EOD school when I first arrived there, I still held a secret clearance in -- with the Marine Corps because I was still technically under my time period for my eight-year contract, although I was on the inactive part of it. The latter half was inactive. The army started paperwork on a clearance for me, and that's what -- that paperwork shuffle took -- why it took so long for me to actually get into a class and start the course. The army granted me, due to the job speciality with the EOD field, a top secret security clearance, which means that I could provide support for the Secret Service to help protect the President, vice-President, and Heads of State that are deemed protection by -- by the Secret Service. We assist them in clearing venues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And let's talk about your deployment and where you served your period in the army. Start back after your school. And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The -- I graduated in February 2001. By April 2001 I was stationed at Fort Benning, Georgia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with the Court's assistance, could we move to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about Fort Benning and your time there.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fort Benning is basically a training facility. They do infantry boot camp for the army. They also have a ranger battalion there. So a lot in dealing with infantry tactics happens at Fort Benning. As part of army -- or the United States Army EOD, we are tasked with providing UXO and IED protection for the continental land mass of the United States. So even though I was stationed at Fort Benning, our jurisdiction was 56 counties in three different States. So Georgia, Florida, and Alabama, where we would help local law enforcement in dealing with possible -- a scenario would be a World War II veteran passes away and a wife finds something in the garage that is a piece of ordnance. They'd call us out to come take care of it. So we provide that assistance in the civilian sector on top of -- soldiers are going through grenade training out on one of the ranges and they throw one and it's a dud, so therefore we -- when I mean dud, it doesn't function as designed. So then we'd have to go out there and remove the explosive hazard so they could complete their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what other things did you do during your time in Fort Benning?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I assisted in training of officers and also enlisted soldiers for UXO and improvised explosive device threats in combat situations. I also provided support for the United States Secret Service in protection of foreign dignitaries and also department of state officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I note six range clearances. What's that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Range clearances are impact areas where they have targets established. And when you consistently shoot at a target with explosive ammunition, you tend to destroy the target. So we'd have to clear the range of all explosive hazards so that the maintenance guys could bring new targets out into the range or impact area safely without causing any injury to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you giving -- given any instructional duties?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Can -- would you mind clarifying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you an instructor?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I taught UXO, which is unidentified explosive ordnance. I taught UXO safety and also awareness of UXOs and IEDs in combat operations, providing that training at Fort Benning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about your deployments.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In September of 2003 we -- we deployed to Iraq from Fort Benning, Georgia. We arrived in Baghdad, flew into Baghdad International Airport in Iraq, and we had six teams organic to the unit. We had four teams that were added to our company to provide EOD support for combat operations in five sectors of Baghdad. The four teams that were added to our company were two army teams and then two navy teams. We basically broke it down with the ten teams to have two teams in each sector providing support, and each sector was basically under a Brigade-size element type of military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell the Court what that is. Explain the gradation.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: A Brigade is -- you could have four battalions within a Brigade. You have four platoons within a battalion. So you're roughly looking at several hundred men, possibly close to a thousand in a Brigade-size element. Depends on if it's an armoured unit or an infantry unit, that dictates basically how many people they have in the units themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell the Court what kind of things you did during your time in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We -- we provided basically what we were doing, the same thing we were doing in Fort Benning except we were doing it more often. We as EOD technicians provide emergency response. When a unit is out on patrol and they roll by or they notice something that's suspicious, we are called out to remove any explosive hazard or render safe any improvised explosive device that's established or set in that area for explosive ambush and destroying Coalition Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell the Court about your missions and -- and what you achieved during that time.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We basically provided support for 1st Brigade, 1st AD. They're an armoured unit based out of Germany. They were based out of Germany; they're not any longer. We ran over 300 missions for them in a six-month period, just my team alone. The company itself in the five sectors of Baghdad ran 2.469 incidents in six months. These incidents could be UXOs which are unexploded ordnance that's laying in somebody's backyard or found just out in the middle of nowhere. We're called in to remove the explosive hazard. In removing it we would make sure that everything's safe for transport, provide transport to a safe disposal area and then dispose of the ordnance. And we -- we provided these -- we basically ran through these missions so that the insurgents would not go along and collect this unexploded ordnance and then turn it into an improvised device and use it against the Coalition Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I have from your resume the removal and destruction of over 8.000 pieces of hazardous ordnance.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't all 8.000 at once. We showed up -- one specific mission we got called out on was a -- a unit was out on patrol and they came across an area where mortar rounds, 60-millimetre and also 81-millimetre mortar rounds were just laying out on the ground, and they gave us the grid coordinate for it and then we rolled out with our security to the incident site, made sure everything was safe to transport, and positively identify everything, all the ordnance and fuses that were there, and then moved to the destruction of that ordnance. And that specific time we found 1.968 mortar rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, did you see any actual combat in Iraq?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes we were fired upon with small-arms fire and also RPGs which are the rocket propelled grenades. And we were also, my team specifically, was explosively ambushed twice in our combat operations in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have any investigative work?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We provided support for the Brigade in the extent of a tasking would come down after a unit had been ambushed, and we would go out and do a post-blast analysis of the incident site and provide any technical reports that we had to directly to the battalion commander or Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so tell us how you would conduct a post-blast analysis.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: When we teach post-blast or response to a post-blast, when we teach that to regular soldiers, we try to tell them to keep out of the incident -- or the actual site of impact or detonation, and upon arrival at the scene, working in a systematic either clockwise or counter-clockwise way of manoeuvring, we work from the outside in, towards the actual site of detonation, providing details of fragmentation that we find. We look at the actual target itself, how the impact -- what type of damage it did to the actual target. That could tell us what type of size or narrow down the size of the ordnance item, looking for components of initiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Initiation components would -- would be your cell phones, your cell phones, your pagers, garage door openers, your key fobs for your remote entry or remote start of your vehicles. Anything with a radio frequency or remote radio frequency can be utilised to initiate an explosive device with the proper electronics to explosively ambush somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of sites did you investigate post-blast? What different scenarios?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We did several that were off route which means vehicles were travelling in a certain direction and the detonation happened to either the right or left side of the column as it was moving in its the -- you know, moving in this direction. We performed post-blast on -- one scenario was -- actual incident was route Pluto, which is one of the main arteries of travel in north-eastern Baghdad. On a catwalk -- they had on the opposite side of the catwalk, they'd hung a 155 with an RF package, and as the convoy was travelling along route Pluto and one of the vehicles passed underneath the catwalk they detonated it on top of the vehicle approximately ten feet above the gunner's head. That specific incident, there were four occupants in the vehicle. Three perished instantly. The gunner was shoved into the vehicle, into the truck itself. When we arrived on screen the vehicle had stopped burning, but the bodies were still on fire inside the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just as part of your combat experience, have you seen people die by fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have. It's not a pretty sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have any post-exploitation examinations of structures?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Depending on where the incident sites -- the post-blasts were, you could have, and there were at times, fragmentation patterns on walls not necessarily inside of a structure, but the wall, pylon, et cetera, became collateral damage or received impact marks from a detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: During your -- your time in -- in Baghdad or other combat operations, did you have opportunity to enter structures that had been -- where explosives had been used?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent of caches were held in buildings and soldiers, foreign nationals on top of Americans had at one point or another gone into these certain areas and accidentally unknowingly set off booby-traps which detonated inside the -- the whole weapons cache detonated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And have you also been in structures that have been attacked by incendiary explosives or just simple fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as part of your regular combat operations and experience?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. These incidents happened overseas and in Iraq and Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, how long did your term in Iraq last?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It was a six-month deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We left in April of '04 and arrived back at Fort Benning. We had approximately two weeks off, and then it was an election year in '04, so we -- we provided support. For the remainder of that year, we provided quite a bit of support for the Secret Service due to the elections and then also completed mandatory army training schools, and then, you know, I got air assault done prior to going to Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about your deployment to Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Almost a year later we deployed from Fort Benning, Georgia, straight into Kandahar Afghanistan. The dynamics there were a little different. We had several -- several units in -- throughout -- spread throughout the country that we provided support to. We did not have the ten teams in five sectors like we did in Baghdad. My team -- myself and my team went to provide support for one battalion, but that battalion's AO is the size of New Jersey. So it's a huge area compared so what we did in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: AO, that's area of operation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. That's area of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I notice that you have the designation of team leader. At this point in time what were your responsibilities as team leader?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As a team leader I was responsible for the missions completed by the team. The -- basically the safety and livelihood of the soldiers that were underneath me was my direct responsibility to -- for us to perform our missions in a combat operation setting without any harm or death or destruction basically to any of our property or ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you have any opportunity for post-blast exploitation work in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. On a much smaller scale. The unit that we were providing support for was an infantry unit based out of Vicenza, Italy, and they would receive or get into fire fights, and I basically did post-blast on wounded that came in trying to depict what type of a -- whether it was a booby-trap or a grenade or, you know, what the munition was that caused the inflictions that the individual had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, why is it important to determine the type of munitions for a post-blast exploitation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Several reasons. You can -- if it's a chemical device that could -- that -- that steers us in a whole different kind of scheme of works as far as how we treat the wounded and then also anybody going back into that area, because most chemical munitions, the chemicals themselves are residual. They stick around for quite a while. We didn't have to deal with any of those. The -- if I can do a post-blast analysis on a booby-trap and I can identify key parts of the booby-trap, I can teach soldiers what to look for when they go back out into sector so that way they don't become victims of the same device again. The same thing with the improvised explosive devices. Much different dynamics in the building of -- of IEDs in Afghanistan compared to Iraq due to the fact that roads could be untravelled for several days to weeks. They utilised victim-operated devices basically. And when I say that, I mean a vehicle would have to go over an improvised switch and set the switch off in order to function the device.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. As opposed to one being set off remotely?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Right. They wouldn't sit there for weeks on end waiting for somebody to come by to -- in certain areas to actually physically hit the button on a remote button on a key fob or whatever. So they would set up a devise that would go off whenever it was triggered, and that could be US coalition forces in a Humvee or a bigger vehicle, or it could be a local national in a truck, or it could be cattle. There was one that was set off by a cow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what security clearance did you hold at this level?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Top secret security clearance throughout my entire time in the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what commendations or medals did you receive in your service?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I received three army commendation medals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3, please of the resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3, please, of the resume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received three army commendation medals, one for each tour overseas and one for the five years that I was stationed at Fort Benning for the duties that I perform there. I received two army good conduct medals. Those were on a -- on basically a time-frame. If you are a good soldier for so many years, you get a good conduct medal. I received a Marine Corps good conduct medal for when I was in the Marine Corps. The national service medal is anybody in the military service that is serving during a time of war regardless if you actually go overseas or not, you get a national defence ribbon. So I received one for the first Gulf War and then one or the global war on terrorism. The Afghan campaign medal is self-explanatory. The global war on terrorism expeditionary medal and the global war on terrorism service medal were for the times that I was in Iraq and Afghanistan. And the NCO professional development ribbons are ribbons that are awarded with the certificates after the platoon leadership development course and the basic non-commissioned officer course. And then the army service ribbon is self-explanatory. It's a ribbon given for service in the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And after your discharge from the military what have you done with yourself?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I've been doing contact -- contract work basically for companies that have department of defence contracts or US army corps of engineers contracts. When I immediately left the service in September of 2007, we did -- I was hired on by a company that we went around and basically cleaned up old military installations searching the ground surface and subsurface clearance of explosive items. I don't -- I don't believe I listed that on the resume. I only ran two or three contracts. They were very short. In May of 2008, I joined a company NEK and went and provided technical expertise for department of defence. The inter-agency would have been JIEDDO, which is the joint improvised explosive device defeat organisation, it's a multi-coalition force, and went overseas and provided technical expertise on exploitation for United States Army units in the area of north-eastern Baghdad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just backing up slightly. What military grade at the end of your last deployment, what was your correlative of rank?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I held the rank of a GS13 for my time with NEK providing support for the army units in Iraq this last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what is a GS13?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's the equivalent of a captain or major as far as officers are concerned in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the equivalent of a captain or major. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on which branch of service you're working with, it's either -- your equivalent to a captain or major. It's in a grey area between the two, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what -- what -- who participated in the multi-coalition force under JIEDDO?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We worked with officers from Canada, officers from the Canadian Royal Army, from the Australian Royal Army. I've worked with British officers and soldiers for training. Specifically for JIEDDO was Canadian and also Australian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at the end of your service were you teaching or training other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Are we referring to while I was on active duty or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay. While I was on active duty we continued to provide training for soldiers that are not within our job skill-set, i.e., your infantry or your mechanics or your armoured -- armoured -- you know, the tanks. We provided the same types of classes, UXO identification and counter-IED and also IED recognition. Basically providing classes for them so that when they go into combat operations they know what to look for and what to stay away from for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about any instruction or training work during your time at NEK?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We were in -- I mean, we provided those types of courses for the soldiers that we were assisting and embedded with in north-eastern Baghdad. My specific skill-set, I provided classes on UXO recognition to soldiers that were there. There were also air force EOD teams embedded with us at the forward operating base that we were actually at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: So worked hand in hand with them to provide training for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would tender him as an expert in explosives, explosive recognition, and post-exploitation of blast exploitation, and tender the CV into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to the CV going into evidence, and clearly Mr. O'Donnell does have some areas of expertise. It seems to me that it's mostly related to the identification of ordnance, unexploded ordnance and the identification of improvised explosive devices. Could ask that the Chamber reserve its decision on whether he's an expert. Because one of the things that I think the Chamber needs to consider is whether his testimony, the opinions that he gives, are within the boundaries of the expertise, because a person could be an expert in one matter, but then when they stray into giving opinions about another matter, they would not be considered an expert. It may be very well, Your Honour, that at the conclusion of his evidence, I will not be contesting it. But I would ask that it be reserved now, and I will explore the matter further with him in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think from a foundational perspective we've met the burden of establishing his area expertise. I think the cross-examination that Mr. Groome was talking about would go to the weight to the testimony that the Court would give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so, Your Honour, is he accepted as an expert in post-blast exploitation? Explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit before we talk about going to Visegrad. And let's -- take us through the standard operating procedures, if you will, for examination of a site post explosion or incident.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: On approaching a scene, you're going to want to get witness accounts of what transpired. You're going to have photographic evidence of the site. You're going to graph off the site if -- if need be to determine and chronologically basically write down where you found certain components of the device. Samples can be taken of -- for explosive residue which can narrow down the type of device that was used as well, and then also collateral damage to either human individuals or property. And the impact that it had on those individuals or property can dictate how the device was established to attack or explosively attack the target. Basically summarise all that information in a type of report with photographs to -- to help support it, and that's -- that's the way we would handle it while we were on active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on active duty how many post-blast exploitation reports did you complete or assignments?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: On active duty I did approximately 15, 14 post-blast incidents in Iraq and Afghanistan. As a GS13 this last tour over in Iraq, we completed two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And what kind of things in terms of -- of collateral damage to individuals or property what -- what do you mean by that? What's important to look for?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Basically you can have a low -- you can have a low explosive or a device that has a minimal amount of explosives, that is a high frag-producing device that can create quite a bit of damage to an individual or an area, a vehicle or property, and -- or you can have a device that has a lot of explosives in it with very little material that would produce fragmentation where the blast overpressure is going to provide all the destructive power to the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before we move too far afield --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Alarid, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Your Honour, we would tender into evidence the CV of Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1D134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at this time could we pull up 1D22-0599.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now -- now your -- Mr. O'Donnell, before we get into the meat and bones of your investigation, tell us about fragmentation and what kind of things can be considered as fragmentation as part of an explosion?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fragmentations is classified as any type of material that is part of the device or moved by the actual explosion of the device that would provide destructive power to either property or personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: So you can have the device itself, if it's in military munition, let's take that, for instance, a military munition, if it's a heavy-cased, and when I say heavy-cased, a thick walled metal material, that in itself is a fragmentation. If you have a thin-skinned type of military piece of ordnance, you're looking for more of a blast overpressure effect instead of fragmentation. If the explosion is big enough, it can -- individuals standing around it can become secondary fragmentation because the blast overpressure tears them apart, makes them or parts of them fragmentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that goes also as well with a vehicle that's on top of the IED or -- or structures that are next to the IED and things like that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Take, for instance, vehicle-born IEDS, improvised explosive devices, that's basically your car bomb. The engine block, the vehicle itself, the axles, the tires, the lug nuts, the seats inside, depending on the amount of explosive used, all of those materials can become fragmentation to help destroy whatever the target is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as part of your -- okay. And as part of the your duties and expertise, are you required to be familiar with ordnance from around the world?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. Going through EOD school, it's probably 50/50 down the line as far as how much US ordnance we study compared to foreign ordnance we study as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And briefly describe the components of an improvised or an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your improvised explosive device is just going to -- in a very simplistic manner you're going to need an explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of things are explosives?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Would you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well are there different kinds in terms of chemical -- is gasoline an explosive?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Gasoline can be used as an explosive, yes. The vapours from gasoline liquid can be used as an explosive. That would be more falling into the lines of an incendiary type of device because it provides so much fire and heat and thermal energy to the actual target.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about something that would deal more with gas overpressure and fragmentation.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In Iraq we were running incidents where - and Afghanistan - where they would take the trigger mechanism and wire it with a battery source, power source, usually batteries, into a blasting cap. When the blasting cap would be put into an actual ordnance, piece of ordnance which was designed to detonate. The ordnance didn't necessarily have to have its fusing that came with it, didn't have to have its fusing on it. The blasting cap itself holds a primary explosive in it, something that's very sensitive to heat, shock, and friction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about a blasting cap.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The blasting cap, mercury fulminate. There's another one, another explosive that they use, it's extremely sensitive to heat, shock, and friction. So an electric current going through it will set it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about a -- what about a lit fuse?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In our training in the EOD school we are -- we're taught basically to provide an explosive train to sympathetically detonate whatever we're trying to get rid of, i.e., you know, the ordnance items in demolition procedures. So you either have what they call a nonelectric blasting cap where you attach that to the end of time fuse, time fuse being a plastic cord with gunpowder through the centre of it, and it burns. Depending on the amount of time fuse you have and also humidity factors, that will basically tell you how much time you have once you light it to get away from the device before it detonates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can in combination with the blasting cap, can a time lit fuse be used to explode other chemical ordnance?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not chemical ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Chemical ordnance would be your phosgene or your lucite or your mustard gas type of ordnance items. Your explosive ordnance, we would run -- we ran incidents regularly where they would use an electric blasting cap or some type of fuse-lit device that would burn down, or when triggered, the current would go through the blasting cap, and that blasting cap was embedded in the actual explosives of the military munition. So you have a projectile that's 105-millimetre projectile. The fuse is screwed into the top of the projectile because it's basically a big bullet and shot down range from an artillery piece. They would scrape away the explosives in the fuse well so that they could glue or plaster the blasting cap into the fuse well, put it up against the secondary explosives or the main charge in the actual device, and when it's set off or they triggered it, it would function just like a regular artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Without the barrel?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Without the barrel. Without travelling down range and without the proper fusing that goes with that piece of ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And tell us the difference between a fire-inducing explosive device versus a gas overpressure-inducing explosive device.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Most of your fire-producing explosive devices are going to be explosive from the vapours that build up, your Molotov cocktail is you're lighting the -- it's in -- I would say an incendiary -- an improvised incendiary device. And you light the fabric that's hanging outside the bottle and when it -- when the glass breaks and spreads liquid everywhere, it's ignited because the fabric's on fire. Your incendiary devices are not as destructive immediately because there isn't that much of a blast overpressure effect. They turn to -- tend to explode and do damage through thermal transfer more than -- than actually exploding and hitting -- hitting the target with a shock wave which is the blast overpressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What causes the fire in an incendiary device versus a regular explosive device?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As long as you have -- as long as you have an oxidiser and some type of accelerant, it can be anything. It can be gasoline, it could be rubbing alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about magnesium, like incendiary grenade?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: An incendiary grenade is basically manufactured to provide just that. It's destructive power through extreme heat to destroy whatever it's put up against.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now if you were assuming an incendiary grenade, would you assume that everything around it would catch fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If it wasn't -- if it wasn't protected or buffered from the actual -- the magnesium or the grenade itself, then, yes, the extreme potential of everything going up in flames is there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now with a regular explosive with gas overpressure, does that start any kind of fire? Would there be a perception of a fire at the outset?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not initially, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Once the explosive -- once the explosive device is set off that -- that instant where the chemical breakdown of the explosives is going on with normal ordnance items, you're not going to have -- you're not going to have fire. With conventional ordnance items you're not going to have fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are you going have a flash?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There will be, yes, you will have a flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: From a layperson's perspective is that flash considered fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not consider it fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm talking about just a Joe Schmo observer.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Someone that's not trained in explosives or the demolition procedures could possibly view that as thermal energy or fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now let's -- I think it's time to move forward to Visegrad and your travel there. But before you -- you went to Visegrad, to Pionirska Street, what kind of materials were you provided, and what did you review before going to the scene?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I reviewed a couple witness statements and also photographic evidence of the site. I don't recall when those pictures were taken, but that was the only material that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to witness statements, what relevant information did you need to begin to think about this from a post-blast exploitation perspective?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: One -- one of the witnesses described getting something detonating or going off and getting physically thrown out one of the windows in the building. And that on top of the witness statement of -- they heard gunshots and screams for half hour to an hour after the incident, the initial incident, led me to believe that an explosive device was used to stun or basically make people incoherent inside the room, and I moved -- I formulated that and moved forward with that once we arrived in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, why -- you know, it -- you were also provided a copy of the indictment against Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I -- Go ahead, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We have to take our time. I just got keyed in because we both speak English, and yet we have -- the translators have to keep up with us, so we'll try and observe a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now you were provided a copy of the indictment, and you are aware that the Pionirska Street charge is centred around the theory that an accelerant was placed on the carpet and the floorboard and that these people were burned by conventional means inside this area. Why is the witness statements with regards to the shootings and the screams relevant in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I feel that the -- the witness testimony or statement, the witness statement of an accelerant being utilised and the room going up in flames is inconsistent with individual -- or the witness hearing for half an hour to an hour after the initial onset of the situation of gunshots and screams. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If you have a room that you're utilising a mass amounts of accelerant and you put people in there and you ignite it, those individuals are going to succumb to smoke inhalation within a matter of minutes, not half an hour to an hour later. And there wouldn't be a need for gunshots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- and just from your personal experience of seeing people die by fire, how quickly were those individuals overcome by the flames that they were engulfed in?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe we're straying outside Mr. O'Donnell's expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply from his personal experience in the field, I believe he has a relevant information with regards to his observations of how quickly fire can really overcome a human being versus the ability to let out screams and whatnot for a significant period of time. It's a minor point but meant to further a theory of modality and liability of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The instances, specifically where we dealt with individuals that had succumbed to fire in Iraq, the -- it didn't -- specifically the one -- the one situation I talked about earlier where the four individuals were attacked in the Humvee and the gunner was pushed into the truck with the explosive device detonating above -- above the vehicle, those -- at least the gunner was killed instantly. The other individuals possibly could have been mortally wounded but not killed instantly. We were on site within 25 minutes, and their bodies were still burning. So I believe it was the detonation and the fragmentation that killed them more so than the fire, but their bodies were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you opine that the witness statements were leaning you towards that an explosive device was either used to, and you said, stun the people, but could people suffer mortal wounds and/or be injured severely in a closed environment like that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. An explosive device, depending on the number of people in that room, an explosive device going off could, even if the individual didn't receive damage to themselves via fragmentation, could have -- could have perished due to the blast overpressure scrambling their brains in their head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go specifically to Visegrad. What did you do? And tell us how you got there and ...

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: My services were requested to come provide exploitation of the house at Visegrad -- or in Visegrad at Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how were you contacted?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Via e-mail and phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: From yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And who -- who provided you the materials and the witness statements?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: You provided me the copies of the witness statements and also the photographic evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And how was your travel arranged?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I travelled with the arson investigators and also Mr. Jenkins from Albuquerque, New Mexico, and we arrived in Belgrade, layover in Amsterdam, arrived in Belgrade on I believe the 28th and decided to get on the road that evening. And then we arrived in Visegrad, I think, at 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about your examination of the Pionirska site.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Upon arrival at the Pionirska site, I -- I with -- withheld initiating my investigation, allowing the arson investigators to go in and do their photographic evidence in there. And basically start and complete their investigation. Mine is -- my -- in going in and basically doing the exploitation of the site, it's not as evasive as theirs are. I was actually digging in the walls looking for fragmentation. So I wanted them to get their photographic evidence on what they found on site undisturbed done prior to me going in and looking for actual fragmentation in the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you know, just from a -- putting it in perspective, the date of the alleged incident is June 14th, 1992. How relevant is it that you're not getting there until 2009?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I think it has everything to do with being relevant. In 15 years or close to 15 years, there will be no traces of explosive residue whatever. Based off the photographic evidence, you can see how the structure itself has just decayed. And it's -- I mean, the whole place has fallen apart. Any type of evidence that would have been left via the device or an explosive device would be gone. Vagrants -- we found human excrement and trash in this area, within the room itself, so it obviously had been occupied by people, a lot of people, over the last 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to tender the report at this time, but we'll mark it for identification and then come back to it after we go through some photographs, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D135, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just to get started, could we bring up Y020-3362. Oh, I'm sorry, 3362. I apologise. My bad handwriting. Could we have 3632 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I just wanted to embarrass you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Identify this photo, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is in front of the house at Pionirska. The bottom room, the door correctly over my left shoulder is the room in question. And that's a picture of me standing outside the structure on the 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We'll tender this into evidence, Your Honour, before we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 29th of January this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring up, please, Y020-3566.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we're going to kind of put you in as if you're walking into the door. And I'm going to show you a series of photographs. And I want you to orientate the Court and describe what we see. And also with the Court's assistance we'd probably be marking some of these photographs as we tender them. So can we give his assistance with use of the pen. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do. The photograph is of the left wall and the back wall of the room. So the far left corner from the entranceway as you walk in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were you able to examine these areas both at a distance and close up?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And just --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And generally speaking, despite the time and distance, did you find some evidence of the potential that an explosive device had been used in this room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. What I found upon entering the room -- in entering the room I decided to proceed to the back wall which is in this picture here and start there working in a clockwise pattern within the room. I found fragmentation marks or impact areas, I should say, impact areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please use the pen and circle what you would call an impact area.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These are the most visible right off the bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- and -- and just tell us what the composition is of the walls as you found them.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This -- this white area here is a plaster, and we found quite a bit of that throughout the room itself. It's obviously deteriorating. When you go up and actually apply pressure to it, it crumbles right off the foundation or the concrete wall on the back behind it. The room itself is in horrible decay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you give us the approximate dimensions of the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Roughly, I didn't -- I personally didn't take measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: But roughly I'd have to say it's maybe 20 by 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's in feet?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. You use the term "impact marks." Why be vague in terms of that or --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Due to the -- the time from the actual incident transpiring and when we were actually able to get there on the 29th and provide exploitation. I'm not going to sit here and say that these are without a shadow of a doubt fragmentation marks or were marks that were made by fragmentation. I use the term "impact mark" because any of the possible individuals that had been in this room over -- or throughout the last 15 years could have possibly made these marks with some type of a device, you know, a steel bar or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And also, how -- how is it relevant that the witness testimony included the firing of weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Because these impact marks could have been made by bullets as well or ricochets.
