So if you have individuals actually shooting rounds into a room, they're going to leave holes or indentations in the plaster and concrete, and these would be areas of possible impacts of rounds or bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we tender this into evidence right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D10 -- I apologise Exhibit 1D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you stated that the room was in extreme state of decay. What was the contributing factors to this decay?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mass amounts of moisture in the room over the last 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of damage had the moisture caused?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Exposed rebar in the ceiling, which I believe we'll see in other pictures, is almost completely rusted through. The right wall which is not currently in this photograph is basically falling apart due to -- due to moisture and the fact that the outside of that wall is covered by nothing but earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's close to the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're right. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm assuming we save --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Assuming we saved the last photograph, we would move on to Y020-3569.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, looking at these, what do these depict to you from that back wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is a picture of impact marks on that back wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have Y020-3574, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what does this depict to you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is very close-up picture of one of the impact marks on that wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what does this picture show you or tell you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This particular picture shows that the point of trajectory was from the ground floor up due to the ridges at the top of the impact mark and the sloping down at the bottom of the impact mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell me based on your training and experience why you come to this opinion.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Due to the height of where this impact mark is in the wall, the trajectory of the object was from the floor upwards, and I believe it's at shoulder level on the wall itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would tender this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we'll bring back Y020-3566, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And put this particular hole in perspective to an unmarked version of the back wall. Okay. Approximately can you tell where this particular photograph is on the back wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. The last photograph would be this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. With the Court's assistance could we use the marker, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last photograph is of this particular mark right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And that was one where you stated that you believed that the trajectory had come from the ground?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct. I realise we're looking at this, you know, two dimensional, but the point of -- or the trajectory would be coming in this direction, ground floor in this area, centre of the room practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, obviously where you've just marked up this picture, we can't see the centre of the room, so you're not saying --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, the picture is not showing where the point of initiation of that possible fragment. The point of initiation would have been somewhere in the centre of the room. This is where that fragment, possible fragment, ended its trajectory in the wall there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please bring up Y020-394, please -- 3394, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what do we see here?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is a picture of as you're walking into the room the wall on the right side of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of -- you had testified a little earlier of the deteriorated state of the right side wall. Does this accurately show that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, the only thing you're not seeing is down at the bottom this picture, which is not in it, all the sediment from this wall as it deteriorates is collecting at the base of this wall itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what other relevances is about this picture? And what is that in sort of the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The -- in this area here, this area here is a piece of tile in the wall itself, and the fragment -- the only fragmentation piece or piece of metal that is not organic to the structure itself was found in this area right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And specifically how was it found, and tell us about what you did.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I noticed an impact mark in the wall here just to the right of the tile. In excavating the impact mark, there's actually a piece of the tile now missing, and it's on the floor. It broke off right in this area. But in following the trajectory and basically the whole of that impact mark, I found a fragmentation piece or a piece of metal embedded in the wall here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you bring that piece of metal with you today?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please produce it to the court assistant, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we would tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm assuming that whatever was recovered is wrapped up in a piece of paper. Could I ask that it be taken out so that we can examine the piece. I would rather not do it. If Mr. O'Donnell wouldn't mind taking it out, and maybe we can look at it through the plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We could even put it on the ELMO as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to get a close-up look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of course. And maybe put the piece on the ELMO after Your Honours have had a chance to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Donnell --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And does the ELMO have the ability to zoom at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, thinking about how you chose to conduct this post-blast exploitation, you said you went to the back wall and decided to move clock-wise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So moving along at that back wall to where it intersects with the right wall and of course the photograph that we just saw last on the monitor, tell us what was going on in your mind as you find this?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: When I first entered the room and approached the back wall, I traced out the impact marks that we've seen on the previous photos. In doing so the plaster was removed from the wall, but I was unable to locate any types of foreign matter at the back end of the possible impact marks. That was not the case here. For whatever reason I followed this impact mark into the wall, and I was able to recover this -- this piece of metal. And the reason it looks the state it is today is because of oxidation of the metal itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, specifically in terms of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Specifically in terms of revealing or reviewing the types of ordnance available to the people in the Yugoslavian theatre, what -- what did they have available to them?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They had several different types of grenades. I brought a manual here with rough pictures of these types of ordnance items. Many of them are actual regular ordnance items and some of them are actually improvised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of improvised, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The -- they utilised the body of the ordnance item that has the explosives in it, but they initiate it by some other means other than the normal fusing that's made or constructed for that piece of ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So can a grenade be rigged to explode using a time fuse?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Actually there's pictures in here of ordnance items that were found organic to the former Yugoslavia area that show actual either wires going into the fuse well or actual time fuse going into the fuse well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I would just ask that whatever book the witness is looking at, could we just have the title of it and some information about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please give us the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This handbook of ammunition used in former Yugoslavia was prepared by the US army armament research development and engineering centre at Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely. We'll put that on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of it is January 2000, and it was prepared for EOD and also other soldiers that -- and military members that were basically having tours over here to help out with the Coalition Forces during the Kosovo Bosnia campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And specifically can you show to the Court on the ELMO some of the improvised grenades and turn to those page, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. Here's a picture of two grenades from this area. The -- as you can see, these are regular ordnance items. The fusing which has the pull ring is actually in the device, so these would function as designed. You pull the ring, throw the grenade. The spoon, which is on this side of the grenades here and here would come off. It's spring-loaded. It comes off releasing the cock striker which would hit the detonator. We have a 3 to 5 seconds burn time, and then the blasting cap goes off inside the grenade exploding -- or igniting the main charge, detonating the grenade itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would this be commonly known as the black grenade? Have you ever heard that term?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- but tell me this: Is the fragment or potential fragment, rather, that you found in the wall consistent with coming possibly from a grenade? And if not tell the Court why.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I can conclusively say that I cannot prove that it is from an ordnance item or from some other type of material, that it could have been there during the making of the foundation of the -- of the house itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: So I can -- I can -- I cannot say that it comes directly from an ordnance item.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And other than the wall being in a deteriorated state, would you have had a better opportunity had you been there much sooner in time?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, due to the fact that the question's been brought up about an improvised device or even just a regular device, the sooner you're on site and able to provide exploitation of a site, time works against you in that manner and answers are -- trickle away as time goes on. So therefore, the time between when the incident happened and when I showed up to do exploitation of the site 15 years later does not allow me to conclusively give any answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now just looking at the photographs on the -- or the drawings on the ELMO, tell us about what it means to improvised grenade -- or hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: These are -- we'll use side, this one to the left. This grenade is actually -- this is a regular military body which is manufactured by some country, and then this is an improvised fusing. This simulating time fuse right here. This is normally a body for a grenade or a booby-trap, and this device is an improvised ignitiation device.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Slide the book up, yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If we look down at these, you can see what that we're trying to depict here is time fuse coming out of a grenade body or booby-trap land-mine body which is used in a grenade form, and it's improvised because it's initiated via time fuse instead of the actual pull -- pull-pin and spoon method that I was talking about earlier off the other grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, why would a grenade get modified from what seems to be a more technically advanced model such as that spoon and pin versus a regular old time fuse?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Most of the time when items are improvised, it's because they're found on the battlefield. They're utilised. You find the grenade bodies, but you don't necessarily find the fuses. So you have to find some way of -- or concoct some way of initiating the device so that way you can use it in a defensive or offensive mode rather than just not having it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the -- with the Court's indulgence, could we copy this particular page and enter it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we would also tender the fragment that Mr. O'Donnell identified on the ELMO into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask -- ask that also the title page of the book also be copied and be made part of the same exhibit so we can retrace our steps here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, understanding that you can't conclusively say that this was a fragment versus something that had actually been part of the pouring of the foundation, but why did you even touch it as a potential fragment?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I removed it from the wall based on the sole evidence of -- basically it lined out that I found at the end of an impact mark. When I say the end, I dug out the impact mark, and there -- that piece of metal was there. So I guess you could say that I concluded that the impact mark was created by that fragment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: With the court's assistance could we have Y020-3557. And did we -- I believe we tendered this picture that's on the screen now into evidence and it was accepted? 3394, yes? Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is a broader picture of the room. Describe what you see here.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This particular picture is a picture of the back wall directly across from the door, and off to the right is the right wall of the room itself. And you can see the sediment down on the floor there that has basically come off of the wall as it's been deteriorating over the last 15 years or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at the tile in the upper portion of the photograph, is that where you located the fragment? And is that the tile before it broke?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please circle that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is the tile here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And although it's at a distance, could you also -- and let's use the blue pen, please, as opposed to the red pen, and circle any other potential fragmentation or impact marks that are visible based on your observations in the room.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is -- right in this area here is the impact mark where I found the actual fragment. And then on the back wall, you can see more impact marks here, here, and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just from one thing certain, would it be as to a certainty that the piece of metal that you pulled out of the wall is not a -- a shell from a firearm? I.e., like, you know, an AK-47 round.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The way the impact mark was going in was from the floor here up in this general correction. That was the impact mark on the wall. Now, if it was an AK-47 round, somebody would have been laying on the floor and shot into the wall that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When -- and besides that also, is there a difference in composition between a -- a rifle shell -- or, excuse me, not the shell but the actual bullet versus the casing to a grenade? Are they different materials?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, the -- your bullets are going to be a more of a malleable type of a metal that deforms upon impact. Your fragmentation is going to be jagged, rough types of very thick metal that would, in a grenade instance anyway, that would basically stay the same shape when they impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we have -- and could we tender this into evidence, please, before we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking up at the wall --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise to the Counsel. The marked photograph will become Exhibit 1D145, and previously the fragment placed on ELMO is Exhibit 1D143, and the second photograph is 1D144.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at the ceiling and the wall on the right, is this the deterioration that you noted earlier?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As you can see in the ceiling, the rebar is exposed. Basically the ceiling's falling in on itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the wall, what is that on the ground at the base of the wall on the right?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Are you -- okay. You're talking about the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah, below the fragment to the right of the blue arrow.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's all the sediment from the wall as it collapses inward as it deteriorates over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at the flooring, it look dark. It looks like it could be burnt wood. Is it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We did not -- myself or -- neither myself nor the arson investigators going in experienced any transfer of carbon from any of the materials on the floor. That would, although it appears very dark in the picture, is actually wet. It crumbled in our hands due to decay. And if you look in the very back corner of the floor underneath the circles - I'll use red on it - this area here -- there's, actually, the wood's dry in that area. That's why the difference in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. So as is where the -- the wood is dark in the foreground. Has that been subjected to fire, based on your personal up-close observation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Based on my observation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we would tender this into evidence and move on to Y020-33 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D145, Your Honours -- 46, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: 3357 -- or, excuse me, 59. And what do you -- actually, that's not the picture I was going to give you, I'm sorry. Let's do Y020-3393. And what does this ...

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the right wall. Again, you can see the sediment at the bottom of the picture where the wall meets the floor. And in this particular picture, the tan material down there or the brown material down at the bottom is the piece of tile that broke off when I was removing the fragment out of the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Will you circle that, and we can tender it into evidence and move on.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Inside that circle is the piece of tile.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And let's have now Y020-3592.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I kind of jumped around the room here. Tell us what we see here.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is a picture of the left wall between the only two windows in the building, or I should say in this -- in this room. The window to the right that has the tiles stacked up in it is the window furthest away from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about -- what do you see in the middle of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: On the wall itself you'll notice that there are impact marks in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what significance is it that the impact marks are in a semicircle around the room? What does that say?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If, hypothetically, if a detonation had occurred from a device, the device was in the centre of the room on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what relevance is it that -- in terms of number of people? I mean, the allegations are 60-plus people were crowded into this 20 by 20 room. What significance is the frag patterns as well as the allegations in relation to number of people in the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The impact mark patterns in the room indicate that there was actually less mass, and when I say mass I'm referring to the amount of bodies, in the room that would have created a buffer between the actual device detonating and stopped the fragmentation or potential fragmentation impacting the wall and making the marks that are currently on the walls now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When -- and in layman's terms, would it be fair to say that where -- fragmentation, where it hits a body, shouldn't hit the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- it's fair to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and conversely, the people in the room would obviously absorb some of the fragmentation from the device.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Individuals closest to it would absorb fragmentation. They would basically become that obstruction between the flight pattern of the fragmentation from its source to the impact marks. And the more bodies and more mass you have in the room, the less effect the blast overpressure is going to have because of the buffer, the mass absorbing of that blast overpressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we tender this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have Y020-3579.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at this, do you see any other evidence of impact or fragmentation marks in this particular portion of the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, there are impact marks prevalent in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please circle them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we would tender this into evidence, Your Honour, following the marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have Y020-3560.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1D148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now let's me ask you this while we're moving the picture: Is it possible that a small explosive device such as a grenade can catch something or someone on fire that is in the immediate proximity to the explosion even for a brief period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: An individual could possibly receive what we refer to as flash burns, but I -- I would say, no, that they don't -- they would not catch fire. They would receive flash burns from the transfer of heat from that chemical breakdown of the explosion or the explosives, but they would not catch fire unless it's an incendiary type of device.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is 3650, and I wanted 3560. I apologise. And looking at this, can you orientate yourself to the photograph. And I'm sorry to jump you around the room. I've gotten out of order on this. What is this?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This picture is a photograph of the right wall and then also the wall that the door is in off to the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you would be standing just inside the doorway looking to your immediate right?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are there any evidence of impact marks on this wall as far as you could surmise even given the deteriorated nature of the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please identify those.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right could we tender this into evidence and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D149.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have Y020-3637.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where is this?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This photograph is of the door frame. As you enter the room, as you're walking into the room, the door opens inward and folds to your left. So this is right behind the door on the left part of the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just for edification, did you see any evidence of fire damage to the wood structuring of the interior of the room such as the door and door frame?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you identify a potential fragmentation impact behind the door?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please mark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have Y020 -- and I believe it would be the next one in the series, 3638.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just to show what we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's a photograph of the same wall behind the door, just the lower half of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, do you see any impact marks, or is there any evidence of fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have last photograph Y020-3398. And could we tender this into evidence, Your Honour, before it's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alarid, I'm trying to get a sense of the time the witness will take up. How much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That was the -- I have maybe one more photograph on my list, and I would tender the report and pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Groome, how long will you be in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's hard to say, Your Honour, but I can safely say I will be well under the time Mr. Alarid used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit 1D151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I believe Y020-3398.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at this wall, what -- what do you see?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the, as you're entering the room, the left wall. This is the window closest to the actual entranceway, and the wall that you see to the right is between the two windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please identify impact or fragment marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the last thing I would call up would be 1D22-0599.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in advance of it coming on the screen, Mr. O'Donnell, did you prepare a report in conjunction with your trip, investigative trip, to Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you prepare this report following the review of the photographs the ones we've seen in court today?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you prepare this report after an on-site visit and inspection of the site known as Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as soon as we get it on the screen, I'm going to have you identify the document. And is it true that the document, including a photo annex, consists of approximately four pages?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you recognise the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do. It's my post-blast exploitation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL

utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. O'Donnell. My name is Dermot Groome, and I represent the Prosecution here. And I'm going to ask you a few questions about your report and your observations at Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it seems from your testimony and your report, there's no question in your mind that there was some type of explosion in the inside of the room that you examined; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you're -- you're not able to say whether it was one explosion, possibly two explosions, possibly three explosions? You're not able to say the number of explosion, are you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Off the witness testimony or the witness accounts --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask -- let's not go to the witness testimony yet. But just in terms of your observations in the room itself, were you able to make a determination how many different explosions occurred in that room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we've already heard you testify that you were there on the 29th of January. You conducted your on-site exploitation. The transcript at page 48 records you as saying: "I traced out the impact marks we've seen in the previous photos." I didn't receive any drawings or tracings. Do you have them with you here today in court?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. It's more along the lines of looking at the trajectory from the centre of the room to where they actually impacted the wall. There were no drawings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when you made determination of the trajectory, you didn't record that in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would that be something you would ordinarily do in a post-blast exploitation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why it wasn't done here?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: One, I didn't have the tools with me. And, two, is it's 15 years after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the trajectory mark change? You've talked about the indications.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The elevation of the floor could have changed due to the amount of debris in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what were the tools that you would have used other than a pad of paper and a pen?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: You could -- you could have used a laser pointer; you could have used strings that you attach from the trajectory hole into the centre of the room to try and face the point of detonation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So given these factors, it seems that your testimony that the explosion occurred in the centre of the room is really an approximation because of time, of uncertainty about the level of the floor and things like that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've told us the size of the room. Give us an idea of how big an approximation are we talking about. If you were to take us back to that scene and you were to draw a circle of the area where the device could have gone off to cause those marks, how big would that circle be?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's going to -- that -- the -- the factors that are not in your -- your question are the amount of people actually in the room and where are they at. So that would throw off any possibility of where I could say the detonation possibly happened. If we actually put 60 people into that room, then we could possibly depict where the detonation, if there was one, possibly happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, are you saying now that you're -- you're not able to say where the detonation occurred or you are able to say?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not to narrow it down to the exact spot, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I understand that. Can you tell us what is the area that you can narrow it down to? How big is the circle that you would draw in that room that you could confidently say to us, I'm not sure exactly where it exploded, but I know it happened somewhere in that circle?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I would say roughly a seven-foot in diametre circle I could draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a 20 foot by 20 foot room I think you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's my estimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the diameter of the circle would be approximately a third of the length of the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, centre of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on page 1, paragraph 4 of your report you say: "To provide the best analysis, sites need to be processed as soon as possible. That failed to happen in this case. After 15 years the site will be vacant of any explosive residue that could have affirmed the presence of an explosive device." Now, in your opinion how long is the time period after which it would be pointless to conduct the examination for residue? Is it a year? Is it two years?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your training was that ever discussed about how long that might be?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are you saying -- and it seems that you're testifying that the impact marks give you a level of certainty that something exploded in that room; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Those along with other facts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So to go and find residue in that room would simply corroborate your -- your conclusion that you drew from the impact marks; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: You have outside factors that have contaminated the site. On the day that we were there, the 29th of January, we found human excrement in the room. Any type of -- the weather, the humidity, the water is going to remove residue --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: -- from the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But my question to you is: If you -- let's say -- did you test for residue?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you had to tested for residue and you found that there was none there, would it have changed your conclusion based on your observations of the impact marks with respect to -- that an explosion occurred in that room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. It wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the presence of residue is really an additional factor but it's not an essential factor for you to reach the conclusion that there was an explosion in that room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not after 15 years, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think the 15 years aspect of it means -- I think what you're saying there, and correct me if I'm wrong, is that after 15 years it's unlikely at that there would have been residue recovered in the room.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's -- that's what my synopsis says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And the decay that you have you've talked about, you've talked about several kinds, structural decay, moisture. You've talked about this excrement, trash, and just the function of time. Have I left any of the factors out that you believe would have made it more difficult to collect residue of explosives?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I can -- I cannot honestly -- I cannot go on record saying what transpired in that room over the last 15 years. There could be other things that are admitted at this time, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But of the factors that I mentioned, those are the ones that you islanded as factors that would have made it improbable that you would have found residue if you tested for it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's conclusive that you would have found residue shortly after the incident. I'm not saying that either. I'm saying that that's one -- one type of product that you're going to look for when you have a detonation in a room or a detonation anywhere, you're going to look for residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain why it might be that we -- we could have gone to the scene shortly afterwards and still not find residue? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Again outside factors: Weather, the amount of moisture in the air, the humidity, foreign matter being brought into -- into the room itself. All that contaminates a -- a site for exploitation. All those factors can destroy the evidence that you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can I take from that that in a relatively short period of time after this explosion occurred, it might have been that the -- there would have been no residue that could have been found? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's not my conclusion. That's your conclusion, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, do you agree with that conclusion? It sounds like --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's a probability, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a probability.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of -- I guess what I'm trying to get at is at what period of time after this explosion occurred would you as an expert believe that the residue is -- has less than a 50 percent probability of being recovered?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's going to depend on what type of explosives were used to begin with as well because the explosives are degrading as they sit inside of an ordnance item. You can have an ordnance item that's 50 years old that has -- in perfect state that has not been subjected to the elements and the -- it has less deterioration in the explosive than one that has been subjected to the weather or the elements. Based off the chemical breakdown of the explosion, when the explosion occurs. What type of explosives out there it depends -- or what was used depends on whether you're going to find residue or not and how long the residue will stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can get a little bit more specific. You placed a book of -- of ordnance from the former Yugoslavia on the ELMO and you opened up to particular pages and they were hand grenades and you pointed to them. Let's -- let me put it to you with respect to the items that you pointed to, the hand grenades that you pointed to. Are you able to give us a range of when the residue from those would -- would have deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I'm not a chemist. I would not be able to do that, no. I can go into a site. I can run tests or pull powder or run swabs for residue, but I would have to send it off-site to somebody to actually do the chemical analysis. That's not -- that's not the function of my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me -- well, let me put the question to you a different way. Let's say you were still in the army and your superior officer said, "Specialist O'Donnell, we have a site where there is an explosion. It happened three months ago. I want to decide whether it's worth sending a team in, to send you in, to do a full exploitation of that site for residue," what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In we were in combat operations, I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why would you say no in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: What pertinent information are you trying to receive out of that? And is it worth risking the lives of men going out to that site to perform this type of an exploitation possibly under gun-fire or explosive ambush? You have to weigh the factors, especially in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so what you're saying now is that before you can actually even do your work as a post-blast exploitation expert there has to be a certain level of security, i.e., there can't be combat in the area to do that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Performing my duties on an EOD team, an explosive ordnance disposal team, as a team and then also a team leader, we were attached security details to provide us escort from point A to point B. And if a commanding officer wanted it done, we would do it to the best of our acts, but again you have to weigh the factors. And is it worth sending -- take Afghanistan, for instance. My team was the only EOD asset in the size of a New Jersey AO, area of operation. So do you want us to spend four hours out there going out three months after the fact looking for residue when we've got two units that are in a holding pattern providing security around two improvised explosive devices or suspect packages which is stopping their missions from continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems that what you're saying is that it's a reasonable decision for a commander or a superior to take that it's just simply too dangerous to send a post-blast exploitation team into an area at this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: What we did our --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we'll get through this much quicker if you can answer my question. If I ask you a question, you begin to tell another anecdote. I'm just asking you --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm trying to get to it, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, is it a reasonable decision for a superior or a commander to say to someone like you, Look, it's simply too dangerous at this moment to go do post-blast exploitation of a particular site?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, returning now to the function of time, at what point do you say to your commander, look, it's improbable that we'll find anything there. Too much time has passed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would just ask for a clarification with regard to "find anything there." Are we talking about residue here or other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Residue.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We not strictly go out to an incident site to perform a post-blast investigation strictly just looking for residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well then --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: And to answer your question, based off of time, if combat -- the area that we -- the detonation went off, say, yesterday, if the area's hot, they are not going to send us. They're not going to send us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about a year after, now the area's no longer hot, would you say to your commander, Look, I'm not sure the value of doing it at this stage, just too much time has passed?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what I'm trying to get from you is what's the period of time where you give that answer to your commander?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It depends on the target that was -- that was, you know -- what was the target? Was the target a State department official that was hit in a convoy or was this a foot patrol with soldiers? And if we're really looking for the evidence of the device and the residue and it's a higher priority and it was a State department official and not just a soldier, then I would say, yes, we'll do it. If it was a soldier, that's just normal combat. And if I'm not on scene within hour or two hours or three hours, if I'm not on scene the same day it happened or within 24 hours, I don't see the relevance of doing a post-blast investigation. We're in a combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to talk to you about the observations that you made on the 29th of January. On page 2, paragraph 1 of your report -- do you have your report in front of you that you can refer to it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you state that you examined the walls of the room and observed the following: "The intact walls of the basement, back, left, and front, had sustained numerous impact marks consistent with damage produced by frag." Now, when you say "frag" that's the type of fragmentation that you've been talking about in your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Frag is a general term for any type of foreign matter that could cause any type of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it would be any type of foreign matter that is propelled by the explosion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, how many impact marks altogether did you find in the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We didn't get a exact count.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'd say roughly 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us the distribution on the different walls you examined?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there was no symmetrical pattern to the impact marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you say there were 30. Was it approximately eight on each wall? Was it 20 on one?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Due to the degradation of the walls and the amount of decay, the wall -- the wall with the windows in it, obviously there's surface area, so I found less impact marks on that one. Wall to the back of the room actually had more plaster that was still a part of the wall itself still attached to the wall, so it was easy to find the impact marks, so I found more impact marks back -- on the back wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say in your report: "Consistent with damage produced by frag," do you mean that this damage is consistent with a fragmentation grenade being thrown into the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, because it could have been any type of a device. It could have been an actual grenade. It could have been an improvised explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it could have been a grenade, it could have been some type of improvised explosive device. Anything else that it could have been or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Had a detonation occurred and depending on the amount of people, I refer back to my comment earlier about mass in the room, the amount of bodies in there, it's likely that any of those -- it could have been primary frag which actually comes from the device; it could have been secondary frag which comes from the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you've so far listed the possible sources as grenade and improvised explosive device; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, when we're talking about the device, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've excluded any type of rigged artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, that would be an improvised explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: So you just said rigged artillery shell. It's not there to function as designed. The initiation system is not there to function as designed. You rig it up, you're going to detonate it on your own, it's not going to travel down the length of a barrel and shot into the room, so, therefore, it's an improvised explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's focus on the fragmentation grenade for a minute. A fragmentation grenade is designed upon detonation to break up into hundreds of small fragments, each being propelled at great velocity away from the explosion with the aim of injuring personnel in the immediate vicinity of the detonated grenade, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's a question that I formulated.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: A grenade is either an offensive or defensive device that is meant to produce a certain amount of frag in a 360 degree area to produce casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's specifically engineered to break up into small fragments and then propel away from the site of the explosion injuring personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the marks that you observed on the wall were consistent with the fragmentation grenade being detonated in that room and the grenade impacting the walls and thereby leaving a mark. We're just focusing on grenades for the moment.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the marks you saw would be consistent with the fragmentation grenade being detonated in that room, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: With it being surrounded by bodies. The I impact marks that I found, the majority of them, and I would say 80 percent of them that I found, were at the shoulder level. And my unity of measure of that is myself I'm 6'2". My shoulder level and above is where I found the impact marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let me see if I can break out your reasoning in that. Your reasoning is that the -- although the fragments would have been dispersed outward in every direction from the explosion, the ones that were travelling at trajectories below shoulder height quite possibly embedded themselves in the bodies of the people there?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the ones that you saw actually make it to the wall and leave marks were ones that passed above their shoulders or over their heads even?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Or between them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or possibly between them.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, what I'm getting at is that the individuals provided obstruction from the source of the detonation to where the fragments would have embedded themselves in the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it's possible for those fragments to have enough velocity to actually pass through the soft tissues of a person. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: When you -- I disagree with that statement only from the simple fact that fragments hit bone and they change direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not talking about the bony tissue yet. But if a grenade were to go off and just hit the flesh of the arm, hit the muscle tissue, not impact bone at all, would it pass through the soft tissues of the body?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fragment -- if you have -- if you had bodies standing around the -- if the device detonated in the centre of the room, you have bodies standing all around it, there is going to be fragmentation found in those bodies. And the ones that are closest to it depending on the amount of explosive used, it's possible that the fragmentation passed through them only to be embedded in someone else behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it would be theoretically possible for a piece of fragment to just simply never impact on anyone's bony structure and simply pass through the soft tissues of one or two people and embed itself in the wall behind them?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I -- I don't find it possible in this scenario because you have the size of the room and estimated 60 people in the room. That's a lot of mass and a lot of nonbony material for a piece of fragment to travel through and then impact itself in the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you've said earlier now that the possible place where it landed could be a circle seven feet wide.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which I take it mean that it could have landed closer to the wall than you're assuming in your answer now, and perhaps it landed in front of only one or maybe two persons deep?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I don't believe my answer's changed. It depends on the how many people in the room. There is no exact number. Anywhere between 30 to 60 people were said to be in that room. And if you have 30 people in that room that's a lot less mass than 60 people in that room. And I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But what I'm getting at is the actual location where the grenade were to land. Let's say it was to land at that outer perimeter of your seven-foot circle. It seems it would be closer to the wall and there would be less people between where the grenade exploded and the wall behind the people. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would you accept that it would be possible for the fragment to pass through perhaps less people, if it had landed in the middle of the room, pass through their soft tissue and made impact mark on the back of the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is -- it's an accurate statement. The walls themselves are so degraded that you wouldn't find -- or I didn't find any impact marks below the waist level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you did find some between the shoulder level and the waist level?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Out of the approximate 30 can you give us some estimate about how many were in that region?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: About five, five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So clearly that -- the fact that more of the impact marks were above shoulder level would indicate to you that there was a possibility that the room was crowned when the explosive device was detonated, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you found the fragment in a wall of the house. I'm not sure what your evidence is on this point. Do you believe it to be a piece of a fragment grenade or do you not believe it to be a piece?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's a foreign piece of material that I found at the end of an impact mark in the wall. I'm not saying what it is. It's so deteriorated and decayed there's no positively -- I can't positively identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I looked at it. Would you agree with me that it's neither lead, nor is it made of copper?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Again, I'm not -- I'm not a chemist, but I would say that it is some type of a ferrous metal because it is oxidised so dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has rust on it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I mean by oxidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, bullets ordinarily would be made of lead, or in some cases that lead would be in a copper jacket, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are no bullets that you're aware of that fire steel or ferrous bullets, are there?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The outside of a grenade, what material is that ordinarily made from?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's a ferrous metal of either steel or tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just a few questions about the mission. It seems from what you've testified to and from my reading all of the reports of the defence experts, that you all went to the scene at the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you had discussions among yourselves about your observations at the scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have discussions about what you observed at the scene after you left the scene?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long were you at the scene?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We were at Pionirska I'd say for about an hour, an hour and a half. Maybe more than that. I had to wait for the arson investigators to finish their investigation before I went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you just tell me the names of the people that you were -- who were present at the scene at the time that you were present?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Defence counsel, myself, Cliff Jenkins, Mr. Cliff Jenkins, and Martin McCoy, and Benjamin Dimas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I don't see anything in your report about doing any post-blast exploitation at the other fire site, the Bikavac site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you visit that site?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I was on scene when they did their investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you not do post-blast exploitation at that site?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Due to witness testimony there was never any question of whether or not there was any explosion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You weren't shown the evidence of one witness about a Molotov cocktail being thrown into the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's an incendiary device, and there is no -- again when you throw a Molotov cocktail the liquid inside the glass jar or whatever is ignited by the flaming rag, the fabric that's on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would that be beyond your expertise to deal with an incendiary device?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's an arson device, not, in my opinion, an explosive ordnance disposal post-blast type of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the reason you didn't do anything at Bikavac is because the witness statements that you -- that you read were speaking about an incendiary device not an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If it was an incendiary device that was set off by an explosion then I would have possibly, had the Defence requested it, I would have done a post-blast, but that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would object to this line of testimony, simply because the truth is he wasn't asked to review Bikavac. But otherwise, because we're all in the same car, he's got to go to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, then let me ask you this: Had you been asked, would it have been possible in your view, in your observations of the scene at Bikavac, to have done a post-blast exploitation of that scene?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, because there's no structure left, just pictures of -- what we have are just photographic evidence of just the foundation, the concrete floor on the ground level. There's nothing else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In fact there's not even any rubble there. It looks like the house was knocked down and the rubble from the house carted away; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: All I saw was the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So no rubble from the walls of the house or roof structure or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I didn't see any, No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it seems that over a hundred -- I'm sorry, about 450 photographs were taken on this mission, and I would like to work with about 50 of them for you -- with you. And given the amount of time it takes to call these up, I asked Mr. Alarid to give you a book of the photos that I would wish to use yesterday to give you an opportunity over night to take a look at the book. Were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed the -- the material yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it approximately 50 photographs in here. Are they all photographs that you recognise from the -- the mission or the time that you went to the scene on 29th of January?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe they were taken by myself or my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are they all fair and accurate representations of the scene as you observed it on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would call up this exhibit. It's MLDT-photo. There's an electronic copy and I've also made hard copies, Your Honour. I think we can just work more efficiently by just looking at the book. So I'd ask -- both Defence have received copies already, so those are for the Judges. Actually, could I ask that if there are copies for Defence, the copies I gave to the Defence yesterday it seems Mr. Dieckmann doesn't have his. And I believe the copy I gave Mr. Alarid did not have the pages numbered yet. Are the pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The pages are not numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I would ask that Mr. Alarid be given a copy as well so that he can follow along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll need a copy of it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that as well. If the usher could save a copy for the witness as well. Is there one for the -- thank you. So, Your Honour, with that foundation, I would tender this MLDT-photo into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the first -- before we look at photos, you've mentioned several times in your testimony blast overpressure.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to explain exactly what is blast overpressure.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The blast overpressure is the shock wave that is formed from a chemical breakdown when the explosion commences.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that if an explosion occurred in this courtroom, that explosion, the shockwave might break the windows behind us, might damage of the walls?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the amount of explosives used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Might even injure us?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If a detonation occurred in this room, yeah, we could lose our hearing. And go from there with -- with more explosives, it's obviously much greater damage done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just -- I forgot to ask you one question about the fragmentation grenade. You testified that it ordinarily doesn't start a fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But that someone could receive a flash burn?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if the -- the carpet in this room were soaked with gasoline and a grenade detonated on the floor, on the gasoline-soaked -- or some kind of flammable fluid-soaked carpet, the grenade could possibly ignite that, no?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Ignite the carpet or ignite the fuel or the vapours?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take them one at a time. Could it ignite the gasoline vapours in the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could ignite the liquid gasoline that's -- or flammable liquid that's still soaked into the carpet?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if people in the room were made to walk in there in their stocking feet and their -- their socks or their clothing absorbed some of the liquid, flammable liquid, could the grenade ignite their clothing?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's improbable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The amount of distance between the actual device detonating and the actual individuals, it's -- it's a what-if question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You're an expert. You're allowed to --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You're the type of witness that can answer a what-if question.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I understand, but I don't have the resources to give you a correct answer. If we did it ten times, it could work five times, it could not work at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But in any case, once the carpet is in flames, and the people, their clothing is going to catch on fire shortly after that anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation, facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe an expert is the one witness who can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness answer if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've already told us that if the carpet were soaked with some flammable fluid, that a grenade could ignite that carpet. And my question to you is accepting your last answer that you believe its improbably that the grenade would directly light the clothing of the people, that if it lights the carpeting, I mean, shortly thereafter if their clothing is soaked in flammable liquid, it's going to ignite as well, maybe not from the grenade but from the carpet; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go back to the photographs. Could I ask you to turn to page 5 on -- in your book. And I wanted to work with the photograph on the top of the page first. And this is a picture of the house that you did your examination of looking at the entrance to the lower room, the ground-floor room in that house; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in is directly above that room, what would be the first floor of the house, there are clay bricks missing from that wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's somewhat a semi-circular shape; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's go down to the bottom page of this -- the same -- sorry, the bottom photograph on the same page. Now, we're looking at the house with our back to the gully --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- and it's hard to see because of the overgrowth, but the two windows of the house are in the ground floor of the house in front of us; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, they're there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the first floor above us with -- where the clay bricks are, we see the same loss of bricks. And at least in the second cavity on the right, we seem to have the same kind of semi-circular shape to the -- to the missing bricks; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
