utterances.text: Now can we turn to page 6, and this is the -- the wall of the house that is directly opposite the one that we were looking at, so this is the side of the house that's facing Pionirska Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And once again, we see the clay bricks missing from the wall in a semi-circular shape of -- similar to the other two sides that we've already looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Are you referring on the wall that faces Pionirska Street or the wall we've already examined that's above the doorway into the basement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, this -- do you not recognise this as the wall facing Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do. This one right here off to the right. That's the wall that faces Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe you're mistaken. So let's go back and take a look at page 5 and see if I can help you get your bearings here. Okay at the top of page 5, that photograph where we can see the door underneath.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The wall that I'm showing you now is the wall that's on the right-hand side. Where we're standing now, Pionirska Street is to the right; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. It runs parallel -- it runs parallel to the building as you're looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So the wall that I was trying to show you on the next page is not the wall we're looking at now, but it's the wall that joins it on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's what I asked you, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if you can look back there and see if you can get your bearings. Okay?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again we have the same damage to the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There's -- there's tiles missing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the last wall of the house, we have a different pattern. And it seems this wall of the house on the bottom photograph of page 6 is the wall of the house that's furthest away from the door. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The picture at the bottom of page 6 is not the rear end of the building as we approached it. The picture of the walls on page -- at the bottom of page 6, these are the two front edges of the building that face you as you approach the dwelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can call up that photograph. It's Y020-3491. And the part of the -- the -- this photograph that I want to draw your attention to is the bottom row of bricks. You see how -- it seems that every brick on the bottom row is broken in half. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that you, during my cross-examination of you, always use a green pen. This way we will always be sure that in response to my questions you use the green pen. I know you have used red and blue. Okay. They tell me that our choices today are just blue and red, so if you would mark it, could I ask you to put your initials on the bottom so I know the ones with your initials were the ones in response to questions from me. So if you would put your initials perhaps in the upper left-hand corner. I won't be working with that part of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to -- oh, we do have green. Okay. So that the record is clear, you'll be making marks in green in response to my questions. Could I ask you to circle the bottom row of bricks in this wall that are all broken.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could I tender that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the question I have for you, when you talk about blast overpressure, if there was a violent explosion in the interior of the room underneath where these bricks are, or underneath the first floor, am I correct in thinking that one of the places where this blast overpressure would have exerted itself was on the ceiling, on the concrete slab above where the people were?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it consistent with blast overpressure that we might see the patterns we've seen here where the walls closest -- or three of the walls it seems bricks fell out or fell in, and on this wall it seems that just the bottom row of bricks all seem to be cracked all along the bottom. Would that be consistent with the effect of blast overpressure?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe the amount of explosives to -- that would need to be utilised to crack every single brick at the corner -- bottom corner of that foundation would have destroyed the dwelling to begin with. So I find it very unlikely that those rows of bricks were strictly broken from just the blast overpressure of the device in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But would the blast overpressure cause that slab that's the ceiling in the room where it happened and the floor of the first floor, would it not cause that to -- would the shockwave not vibrate that slab?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm not saying it wouldn't vibrate it, but to cause that amount of damage especially when you have two windows down in the bottom dwelling area or living space on top of a door, I find it very unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Any idea, then, based on your expertise what would have caused every brick along the bottom row to crack like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can he answer the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have an answer for that? No, I don't. I'm not a carpenter, so I wouldn't know why that would deteriorate the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you mean you did --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: And again the upper parts of the building were not in the area that my exploitation was being needed. It was strictly the one room down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you didn't look at the rest of the building?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's -- no. There was nothing to look at from my -- from my standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you made that determination without looking, or you looked and made a determination that there was nothing of significance when you looked?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I walked the perimeter of the building and saw that there was no significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so it's your evidence that there's no significance whatsoever that the clay bricks on the walls directly above where an explosive device was detonated, it's your evidence that that's not significant?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's not -- I don't believe it's significant due to the amount of concrete that's surrounding in the slabs of the room below. And you have the two openings of the window and the doorway to vent the blast overpressure after it bounced around inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you measure the thickness of the slab?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. There's no way to tell. There's so much grass. As you look in the pictures there's grass and vegetation and a tree growing in the middle of the house. There is no way to tell how deep or thick the concrete is at different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me move to a different area now. Can I ask you to turn your book to page 9. Page 9 has pictures that you took of the windows in the room where the detonation occurred. Now, am I correct in saying that the -- the two photos on this page, the top picture is the window on the left immediately behind the entrance door, and the photo on the bottom is the -- is the window to the right furthest from the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If you walk in and face the left wall, you're correct in that. The window up top is to the left closest to the actual entrance to the room, and the photo on the bottom is the one furthest away from the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the pictures that you took of the windows, the window jambs are missing. The wooden frame that holds the glass is gone?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection. Assumes facts not evidence. There is no indication, I believe, within the record that there was glass windows within those openings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If Counsel rereads VG-18 or VG-13, I think there's ample testimony about what was in these windows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But again, sir, you're allowed to answer even hypothetical questions. If there were glass windowpanes in this, in the frame, is it possible that blast overpressure could drive out the frames, could push them out?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Possible, but I highly doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why do you highly doubt it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Because the glass would have broken which would have vented it immediately. If this was boarded up and all the same material, the same wood, was closed -- closed off this entire portion, then I would say, yes, it's probable that the blast overpressure of a device could have pushed out the entire framework including the frame around the stonework. It's path of least resistance. The glass breaks there goes your blast overpressure out the window. It's not going rip away -- let me rephrase that. It's unprobable that it ripped it out and pulled it to the outside of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So then if it's not here now, it seems then that someone would have removed it, then, sometime after the blast.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, it seems that it has to be one or the other. Either it was knocked out as a function of the blast, or it was taken out by someone who manually took it out of the window; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: One or the other. But I don't believe it was blown out of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about the door? Is it the same possibility for the door? Let's say the door was closed and locked or sealed in some way. Is it possible that the blast overpressure would push out the door including the door jamb?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible but, again, the door is made of a thick material, so the door itself would come off prior to the framework being ripped out of the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your belief that the most probable scenario is the door would tear off the hinges before the entire door frame would go --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- out?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Path of least resistance. The door is the weakest link in the chain, and it would have been blown out without removing the door frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that part of your -- one of the jobs that you had was in construction. When you looked at this door and this doorjamb in the building, do you believe it was the door that was there at the time of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No and my expertise in construction was in a deep tunnel project with a jackhammer on the back of a mole machine, no carpentry skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What made you come to the conclusion, though, that it was not the door or the doorjamb that was there at the time of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe that misstates the answer. I think he was qualifying his construction experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you again. Do you think this was the -- this was the door that -- and the door frame that was present during the -- the time of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask for an instruction to Counsel to cease with these incessant objections with respect to speculation. He is a witness that is allowed. I can put to him an explosion on Pluto, and he's allowed to answer that. He's allowed to speculate. He's a qualified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Alarid. They are quite pointless in relation to this witness. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, how can this witness say when this door was put or not put, whether it was original or not original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him say it whether he can say it or not, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tell us about the door. Do you have an opinion as to whether it was the original door or not?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you're unable to say?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your conclusion about there being no fire damage on door really has no relevance; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I was never asked about fire damage to the door. That's not my area of expertise. I'm not an arson investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Weren't you asked that on direct examination?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, not to the door, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The doorjamb?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just have a second. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I don't believe I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, when you were shown photograph 3638, it was the doorjamb. And I'll find it on the transcript, but your testimony records you as saying there was no fire and there was no impact. Do you --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I was asked about impact marks on the concrete surfaces near the door. I was not asked about fire on the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just see. It's on page 60. Let me just call it up. I apologise for taking this time, but page 60. Mr. Alarid asked you -- this is what the transcript records you as saying. Page 60, line 9. "Q. Now, do you see any impact marks, or is there any evidence of fire?" And your answer was: "A. Neither." Do you wish to change that answer now?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. There's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to what? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. Let me read the question before. Question by Mr. Alarid: "Q. And just to show what we're seeing -- "A. It's a photograph of the same wall behind the door, just the lower half of the door." And then you he said: "Q. Now do you see any impact marks, or is there any evidence of fire?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that appears to relate to the wall behind the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is -- well, let me clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When Mr. Alarid asked you just the lower half of the door?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. The observation that I was making off of that photograph was to say that it's the same wall from the previous picture, it's just the lower half of the wall. You're looking at a picture of the lower half of the wall, lower half of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So what is your evidence now with respect to your observations of the door and the doorjamb? Is it that there was evidence of fire on it, or there was not evidence of fire on it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to make that assumption or any speculation thereof because I'm not an arson guy; I'm an explosives guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I mean I think it's -- you don't need to be an expert. Isn't part of all of our common experience as humans that we have seen burnt wood, whether it be a log on a fireplace or, you know, a piece of wood that's burnt. Are you saying that you have no impression of whether there was fire damage on the door?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Call up -- I think it's all of these are Y020. 3637.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now is this the -- this is the photograph we were speaking about and --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's the top portion of the doorjamb door and above someone's head on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Behind the door as it opens up into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your evidence with respect to whether there's fire damage on this doorjamb?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there doesn't appear by this photo to be any fire damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we zoom in. There's a piece of wood sticking horizontally at the top of the door. Could I ask that we just zoom in there. Maybe zoom in even more. Maybe slide up to it now. Now, when I look at that piece of wood, I see one side appears to be black, and the underneath part seems to be white ash. Is that not fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. Lack of foundation with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please stop. Please stop, Mr. Alarid. Please stop. You are irritating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... then the Prosecutor is testifying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on this photograph, I cannot make that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at another one. Could I ask that you look at 1D151 in evidence. It was admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we zoom in on the edge of the door frame there. Any portion of the edge. Not the door itself but the edge. You'll see the -- the unpainted wood and then the black edge. If we could zoom in even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Donnell, it seems looking at this that the entire edge of the door appears to be -- have burnt. The wood seems burnt. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I disagree. When we were in the room itself, none of the wood that we looked at, none of the wood that we tested as far as touch, feel had any fire damage whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now you're --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We found a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you're saying you're competent to recognise fire damage?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I am saying in picking up pieces of wood there was no charcoal transfer from the wood to my clothing, to my boots, to my gloves, any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I agree -- I accept that it's possible that a piece of wood could be burnt and time has elapsed and it was no longer possible if you were to contact it with your clothing or your hands, there would be evidence of ash. Accepting that. But that's not the same as saying there's no damage caused by fire to the wood, is it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now these are pictures that you took. So we're relying on your observations and the pictures that you took. Now, I want to show you -- I mean, as good as this technology is, it's still not as -- it doesn't have the definition of an actual photograph. So these are the photographs that -- that Mr. Alarid provided me. I'm going to ask you to look at Y020-3639. It's a photographic print of the picture you took.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you that you take a look at it. And you look at the piece of -- of -- again, this is the piece of wood that's horizontal. It's in the top edge of the door. Is it not fire damage on that piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I cannot conclude that from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that it be shown to the Court and to Defence counsel, and I'd ask that it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object only so much as we have the electronic copy. I don't see the necessary relevance of this print taking some precedent over the digital copy that's on the screen in front us. They're identical photograph. I think we can all stipulate to that. But I think that trying to characterise the printout as showing something that the screen does not would be improper in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The objection is without merit. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir if we could -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. That's Exhibit P267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we could return to the lower photograph on page 9. We can see the doorjamb. There's no wooden structure or window jamb --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Are you referring to your book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually it's your photographs and it's the books that I put --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honour, we would object to characterising them as Mr. O'Donnell's photographs. They were tendered. They could be the arson investigator's photographs; they could be Mr. Jenkins photographs. They were separated by memory card when they were tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Mr. Groome, please use the correct description.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the photograph that you took?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I can't say if it was or not. A lot of us -- we took photographs of the same material. You were talking about a photograph just a second ago on page 9 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I want to ask you a question about that photograph.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay, that's the window, not the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yeah, I misspoke what I said [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Just making sure I'm tracking where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is no wooden window jamb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. There's a complaint which I have heard of overlapping --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- between counsel and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The window that we see here has no wooden window jamb in which glass could be affixed; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What we do see are clay bricks mortared into the window lying sideways; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's a possible observation. I don't know if they're necessarily mortared in there, but they're within the window jamb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we accept the evidence of -- or the observations of the survivors, they weren't there on that night. So it seems that logic would -- would draw us to the conclusion that someone has attempted to make some use of these rooms, that these bricks were put here for a purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- it's definitely accurate to say that somebody has occupied this dwelling since the night of the incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you say "someone," and I want to explore that assumption with you. The bricks are put in in such a way that in the cold winter, and it gets very cold here in Visegrad during the winter, the wind would simply pass through the blocks the way they're put in now; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That if someone were to put these blocks in the window because they wanted to inhabit it, to live in it, common sense tells us they would have put them in the way they're meant to be put so that there is no gap; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Sure. I don't understand where you're going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you agree with me that if someone were going to dwell in this house and wanted to put these bricks here to make it a dwelling, they would have put it, the bricks, in a way that blocked the wind, not permitted the wind to come in; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the blocks put here seem more consistent not with someone inhabiting it but someone keeping animals in this room after the blast?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for -- well, calls for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I disagree. The window that you're looking at right now has possibly a five-foot drop further to the ground outside of it than the window closest to the door does. [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It seems -- it seems the French translation -- it seems the French translation is coming across the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I just got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me now take you to page 10. Now, both of the photographs on page 10 are photographs of the ceiling in the ground floor space of this house; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the top photograph is the ceiling just immediately outside the entrance door. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's difficult to stipulate that that is based off of this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, then the bottom photograph, are you able to say from the bottom photograph whether it is actually inside the room or outside the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The bottom photograph I could say is inside the room. If you look in the bottom left-hand corner, you can see the top framework of a window. So therefore that tells me that's the ceiling inside the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now when you were doing your post-blast exploitation, did you examine the ceiling of the room as well?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As far -- as far as what? Look for it for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the things that you look for when you do post-blast exploitation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, from your description of what happens when something's detonated, it seems that the ceiling might even have been a better place to look for impact marks because people wouldn't have blocked the path to the ceiling?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct in that statement, but the -- the amount of decay to the ceiling prevented us with moisture coming in -- water was actively dripping from the ceiling. It prevented us from doing any -- any exploitation of the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, am I correct in saying, according to your observations, there was more rebar exposed inside the room than outside the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And they both would be subjected to the same level of decay. In fact it could be argued that the ceiling of the portico, of the area just outside the door, might even be more exposed to the elements; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would object to relevance and outside the witness's area of expertise, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just put it very simply. The area of the ceiling just outside the door, in the portico area, had less rebar exposed than the area inside the room itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, taking what you've told us about how blast overpressure works, is it possible that a blast going off in the room, that the shockwave up to the ceiling could have played some part in the amount of concrete material that is missing here and exposing the rebar?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at page 8, and these are photographs that you worked with on your direct examination. I don't recall at the moment which exhibits they are now marked as. These impact marks, can you tell us approximately how deep they are?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fractions of an inch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you be a little more precise, a half inch, quarter of an inch?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They went through the plaster on the wall and then met with a more dense material of the concrete behind it, so, therefore, they didn't travel as far in. So the plaster of the wall could have been a 16th of an inch thick, and it definitely went through that, and it left small indentions on the actual concrete it he have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The blast impact mark that we see at the bottom seems to have some blackening inside it. Is that of any significance to you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be your understanding that it it's simply dirt or some other foreign matter?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This particular photograph is the one where you said you were able to calculate a trajectory from; is that correct? That's the bottom photograph on number 8.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The probability of the trajectory is more accurate than actually calculate the trajectory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, from your testimony you mentioned two impact marks where you estimated the trajectory as the explosive device originating somewhere below and moving up towards the impact marks; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there only two of the 30 impact marks that you were able to make that estimation? Or were there more?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Those two specific, I came to that conclusion. I've also said that these impact marks could have been made by anything. That's in my testimony. That's in my written report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I guess what I'm trying to get at is, were any of the impact marks that you saw consistent with just the direct horizontal path from the explosion to the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were there -- how many showed this upward trajectory?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'd say maybe about half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And of the remaining half, did any show a downward trajectory?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I did not -- I did not witness that there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The fact that you saw half of the impact marks with an upward trajectory and half with no upward trajectory, can we conclude from that that there was a probability that two explosions occurred in this room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible, but witness accounts only say one explosion, and then -- and half hour to an hour of gunshots and screaming. So your impact marks that are -- appear to be straight, parallel to the floor, could possibly have come from weapons instead of a device exploding in the room itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, am I right in thinking that a fragment that travels at high velocity with enough speed to impact a wall of concrete and leave a mark like this, that at least in some of these there should have been whatever that particle was imbedded in the concrete; right?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Should have been. I didn't find any other than the one fragment that I produced for the Court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what percentage would you would expect to find fragments embedded in a wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I don't have an answer for that because I don't know what the device is made out of. And I've said in my testimony that the fragment that I brought was not organic to the foundation. Meaning it wasn't a piece of rebar. So it could have been any type of foreign matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it seems that it was a ferrous material which you've told us is also the same type of material that's used in hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's possible the fragment you found is a hand grenade fragment; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question to you is that if it's likely that the particles, the fragments, would embed themselves in the impact marks that they make, that seems to suggest that they were removed, no? At least in some of these impact marks.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It didn't look like anybody had gone in there and tried to excavate any of the impact marks prior to me being there. So as far as why we have impact marks that there are that should potentially have fragmentation in them, I don't know why it's not there. And I've also stated that these impact marks could have been made by other things other than an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's -- you're here as our explosives expert, so let's focus on that. Is it possible that had some of the fragments embedded themselves in the wall that if somebody went into this room and washed it down with a powerful fire hose that that could dislodge some of the fragments that you would have expected to see in the holes. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that you be shown Y020-5579. Just looking over my notes, I see that was adequately covered on direct examination. So I ask that it not be called up. There is really no need for me to go into that again. I'd like to talk to you about your conclusions now of your report. In your report you say: "There was some kind of explosive device used in this incident." So you state with a level of scientific certainty commensurate with your experience and expertise that an explosive device was detonated in this room; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I have Retired Colonel Travers next to me and another person that I've consulted on this. May have been your superior, I don't know, in Afghanistan, a Lieutenant-Colonel Ray Lane, let me give you his title, and see maybe he's someone that you know. He was the Chief of Operations for counter improvised explosive device branch, a senior advisor to the commander of the force in Afghanistan. Would you have had contact with someone like this, the Chief of Operations of --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One of the things they've suggested I explore with you is fuel air effect. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to tell us what is the fuel air effect?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: If -- I believe you're referring to fay [phoen] bomb type of -- is that what we're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me give you my understanding --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Fuel air dispersion and ignition of that. Is that what we're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're putting to me now. So let me put to you what I think the definition is, and please correct me if -- if I'm misstating it. Am I correct in stating that a fuel air effect is when flammable vapours present in the air ignite causing an explosion. It would be similar to holding a lit match over a can, open can of gasoline?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that's the fuel air effect?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's not the can of gasoline that's exploding --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's the vapours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- it's the vapours that have accumulated. And that's why on every gasp pump in the world there's a warning not to be there with an open light; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the case of an enclosed space, the fuel air effect can be very great. So for an example, in the case of a house which has a natural gas leak, if the gas vapours accumulate in the house and are not allowed to escape, if they are ultimately ignited by something, you can have a catastrophic destruction of the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the case of volatile chemicals, would high heat, high humidity contribute to the rate at which these volatile chemicals are transformed into flammable vapours? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Are you asking is it going to accelerate the process the liquid goes into a vapour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if we had a can of gasoline in the winter and we had a can of gasoline in the summer, we could expect greater vapours to be created during the summer?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, early in your remarks, and you've mentioned it several times in your answers to me, the importance of witness accounts. I think you said that's one of the first things that you try to do when evaluating a site is to see what the witnesses say. Now, there has been evidence from witnesses that there was some sort of volatile chemical soaked into the carpet of this room when they entered it. Would the fact that it was a summer night, that approximately 70 people each giving off their own body heat, the fact that the windows were closed, the door was closed, might this all contribute to the potential for a fuel -- fuel air effect explosion in that room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would closing the door of the room also contribute to the concentration of flammable vapours in the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't have a venting source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, accepting that scenario, what might happen if someone opened that door with an open flame in their hand, perhaps a match, perhaps a Molotov cocktail? What would happen if a person was at the doorway, opened it with some kind of lit flame in their hand?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They could possibly expect an explosion in their face.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From the vapours in the room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be likely that the -- the source of ignition would begin at the flame in the person's hand; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's quite possible that they, themselves, might be injured at least in the hand in which they're holding that lit frame?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That size of room that possible scenario they would be lucky to just walk away with just injuries to their hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And there could be a terribly violent explosion because of fuel air effect?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It could be as powerful or perhaps even more powerful than a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In that room it would possibly be more powerful than a hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that explosion would essentially be a cloud of flame that entirely -- entirely engulfed the room and all of the participants in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Momentarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And such an explosion would also cause blast overpressure; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Not to the extent of an actual chemical breakdown of an explosive, but, yes, it would cause blast overpressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you to look at page 25 of the -- of the book that you have before you. Now, these are pictures from the ground floor of that house, pictures taken by either you or one of your colleagues on the 29th of January. Can you tell me precisely where these pictures were taken?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe this is in a very small crawl space. If you're looking at the entrance it's kind of tucked up to the right of the door, if you're looking at the entrance of the room. It's outside the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask that we split the screen. And on the other side we call up photograph Y020-3344. While that's being called up, would you agree with me that this is clear evidence of fire-damaged wood?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the number again is Y020-3344.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We're looking at the house. We're looking at the entranceway. If I ask you to circle the area where this wood was, would you be able to do that on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So could I ask you to take the pen. Hopefully it's in green.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'll wait for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to begin by putting your initials somewhere, not on the house, and then when you're able to circle as precisely as you can the area where this wood was.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's tucked up in this area over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask you just simply, so it would be easier for us later on, just to put "burnt material," or "burnt wood," something to indicate what that arrow means.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's -- that's -- actually, maybe if -- if the court usher would remain there. Just so the record is clear, we've gone away from green and we're back to blue, but in case these are marks that you made in response to my questions. Now, could I ask that that exhibit now be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, how much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I only have about ten more questions, Your Honour. I think we should move rather briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I'd like to try to complete this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple more photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, are you going to be re-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I look at maybe using two photographs for clarification and the questions that it would take to clarify two photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I ask that I tender the picture of the house where Mr. O'Donnell has made some markings, then once that's done could I ask that that be removed. And if we could zoom in on the left-hand side of the top photograph. Okay. If we could just go back to one image on the screen and please focus, enlarge the left-hand side of the upper photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's take a close look at this burnt material. There's no question that this is severely charred material; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it appears -- you see the piece of wood sticking out that does not seem to have any damage from fire?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to circle that, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I right when I look at this, I mean, you were there, you saw this up close, to me when I look at that it seems that that is a thin strip of wood that has been fixed to the concrete foundation horizontally so that another -- something else could be attached to it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's the material that was attached to it that seems to have sustained the burns, not this piece that it was affixed to; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The edges look like they're fried, but, yes, more damage to what's affixed to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I know that as furring strip. Are you familiar with that term furring strip?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Furring strip would be horizontal pieces of wood that something is attached to. I want to show you another photograph. Could I tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I call up -- can I call up a Defence exhibit -- well, before I call it up as a Defence exhibit, will it be possible for the witness to mark in green? If not, I'd call up a fresh copy so there's no confusion. Perhaps let's not take any chances and we'll call up a fresh copy. So I would call up Y020-3398. And I want to tender this into evidence. So this will be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was admitted as Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see that it's been erased. I don't want it erased. What's that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's saved already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's saved already. I'm finished with this exhibit, and could I call up Y020-3398. That's Y020-3398.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is a photograph that you already worked with with Mr. Alarid. What interests me at this point in time is you see the strip of wood underneath the window?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's not the same type that we were just looking at, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's -- I mean, it's a piece of wood. Are you asking for me to narrow it down if it's oak or elm, or -- it's a piece of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Okay. It's a piece of wood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it of the same proportions as the other piece of wood we saw; namely, a thin strip of wood affixed to the concrete foundation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: While on site that piece of wood actually looked like it was embedded in the foundation, not strictly attached to the surface, it looked like it was a part of the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that you circle that piece of wood that we're talking about so that it will be clear for future reference.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want my initials?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last photograph that I want you to take a look at is Y020-3564. Now, here we see, do we not, a piece of similar wood not affixed to the wall but leaning up against it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct. Bottom left corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to circle that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that as you found it, or was that removed from the wall?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That was as I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit. And I ask that Exhibit P269 be called up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just have one more question for you, Mr. O'Donnell, when the picture is placed on the screen. Sir, given -- when we look at P269, given that we see this narrow strip of wood relatively unblemished behind this severely charred wooden material and we find similar wood inside the room where those people died, you have no way of determining whether or not the entire original interior surface of the wall was charred in this way, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. With regards to this exhibit on the screen here, is this the book, and can we go page by page and not have to use the separate numbers? Is that how it was working?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The book is P265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this being the book of the Prosecution's pictures that we've all been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear. It's not the Prosecution's pictures; they're Defence pictures organised in a particular way by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed. And please remember we are trying to finish by ten past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's why I want to get to this. Can we go to page 5 as referred in the picture book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'd briefly like you to take a look at page 5. That's page 4. Oh, I'm sorry. The next page, please. Now, looking at the photographs, Mr. O'Donnell, the Prosecutor mentioned the -- the removal of bricks kind of in this semi-circular pattern over both the front door on the side, and I got the impression that he didn't quite go out and ask you, but I got the impression that the theory was whatever blast might have been in that basement room was severe enough to knock out the walls. And could we move to the next page, please. And looking at the photograph knocking the bricks and breaking the bricks along the -- where it attaches to the foundation. Now, have you dealt with explosions or explosives that have -- or were significant enough to blow out walls and crack foundations?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but what is problematic is when you put an explosive device of that size in a confined space does that amplify or decrease the explosive charge?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: When you have an explosive device inside of a confined space, it's going to, I guess -- look, would you mind clarifying just so that I can answer correctly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I guess this: Would a grenade or even two grenades or three grenades thrown in that bottom room be of sufficient explosive power to crack the foundation and blow the walls out in the upper structure?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No. Negative. As Prosecution talked about a 155, if a 155 was in there, it could have brought all the walls down on top of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But by the same analogy what would happen to anyone in that room?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: With the 155 or the three grenades?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about 155?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: You would have been very hard pressed to find bits and pieces of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about hearing screams and shots for the next 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about anyone surviving?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just simply put, I mean, let's not -- let's not qualify it by 155 or even three grenades. An explosive charge sufficient to blow out the walls of the upper story and crack the bricks around the foundation, would we be finding survivors in that basement?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, we would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would any survivors have made it out the door or the windows?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, they would not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we turn to what I think would be page 13. You were shown these pictures a little bit earlier. And I say it's 12 in the book but -- as numbered but 13 for e-court. Do you recall looking at these pictures?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I think the discussion was surrounding the door and the door frame and would it have blown out. If the door had been shut prior to the explosion, just assuming grenade-strength explosives, would we have expected the door to be blown out or the frame attached to it to be blown out?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your weakest link in the three entry points to this room the windows and the door, the windows if they were -- had glass in them would have been the weakest link and all the blast overpressure would have gone out that way, just from we're talking about grenade-sized explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just considering that blast overpressure as it relates to the picture we saw of the ceiling, is it possible that the blast overpressure could simply weaken the structure of the concrete causing an acceleration of deterioration by other ambient means such as moisture and water, but not necessarily cause the damage way back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that the witness not be led?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're doing a little leading there, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge. I'm just trying to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Looking at the ceiling and seeing how it collapsed inside and exposed the rebar, obviously moisture, you testified moisture was coming through the ceiling. But my question is, is it possible that the blast overpressure weakened it back in 1992, but the collapsing or the deterioration happened later?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And looking at the -- could we put both pictures on the screen as they are from that page as opposed to zooming in? Now, just looking if -- if -- if on a hypothetical the door frame had blown out, would you expect to see plaster and concrete in front of the wood as you do in the picture?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Because it -- the wood would have pushed the plaster and concrete out of its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now we see a lot of black stuff up on the ceiling and we saw it around. Did you have an ability to make an observation what that black stuff was?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe I phrased this in cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We're under the same porch where the wood was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did. And I say we as the entire team, the arson investigators and also Mr. Jenkins and myself, we deduced that the black substance that you see on the ceilings is mould of some type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, there was testimony that the old -- an old man survivor of the fire was blown out an open doorway. Is it possible that someone could be blown out by blast overpressure, especially an older man, maybe a smaller man?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. From a grenade?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Donnell. That concludes your evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Earlier today I indicated that the Chamber will hold a hearing tomorrow morning in relation to a particular matter, and I said that there would be a discussion. The Chamber has since developed its position in relation to this matter. It will instead give a ruling, and it may entertain one or two questions by way of clarification. So I just want to make that clear that the Chamber will give a ruling on the matter in the morning. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask, does the Chamber wish anyone else from the Prosecution aside from myself to be here to address those questions to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No. I believe you're perfectly competent, Mr. Groome. We are adjourned. Let me just clarify one other matter for tomorrow, the position with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But other than that, Your Honour, according to VWS, they may need us -- because of here state, we may not be able to proof her until Monday. And so that's their qualification based on her representations, not mine. But she -- and the travel time. But other than that, Your Honour, you know, assuming we proof on Sunday, we would have a witness for Monday. But if we don't, we wouldn't have a witness until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of March, 2009, at 8.50 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
